As a result of divisions in thinking, a free-standing ANSI Committee, ANSI
Z359, sponsored by the American Society of Safety Engineers (ASSE), was
established to address fall protection for all industry areas, except construction and
demolition. The charter and standing of the American National Standards Z359
Committee on Standards for Fall Protection was accredited by ANSI on January 6,
1988. Its goal was to create a standards matrix to cover systems, anchorages, and
testing for the following: (1) fall arrest; (2) work positioning; and (3) rescue and
evacuation. The first standard, Z359.1-1992 (reaffirmed 1999), covered fall arrest
systems and did not permit the use of body belts for fall arrest. The Z359.1-1992
was the most advanced free-standing, general industrystandard, at the time. The
Z359-2007 set of standards, dubbed The Fall Protection Code, continued that advance.
Up to 18 fall protection standards are being developed as the Z359 Code has been
unbundled into component and engineering standards, allowing for more timely
introductions and improved opportunities for updates.
History of the ANSI Fall Protection Standards
The need for fall protection standards activity grew out of several preexisting
conditions. Between 1970 and 1980, fall protection equipment and methods
advanced beyond the coverage of the U.S. standards and government regulations
published up to that time. That trend continued through the 1980s. Reform of fall
protection standards in industrialized nations throughout the world, and drafting
of a new international standard, got under way early in that decade. In 1983, the
United States joined the ISO effort on fall protection.
At the same time, the pertinent construction industry standards were due for
revision. There were a few specialized standards that addressed specific industries
or specific equipment and techniques. However, there were no broadly applicable
U.S. standards for much of the equipment, and the methods in commonplace
industrial use, or for occupational or non-occupational fall protection. A task force
of the ANSI Safety and Health Standards Board recommended formation of a
free-standing committee to address the subject of fall protection. The ANSI’s
TAG, which represents the U.S. fall protection interests to the ISO, acted upon the
Safety and Health Standards Board recommendation and initiated formation of
the Z359 Committee. The ASSE assumed the Secretariat.

replacement service 10 feet overhead next to a column. Planning and coordination
is a must for access for repeat visits and especially for single visits. Wiring for the
internet and telecommunications has made utility access a significant hazard above
almost every corridor when old wires are not replaced and new wires follow no
plan for their location.
Often, contractors are brought in to perform elevated work. It could be a
maintenance contract that requires the contractor to climb unprotected towers
and stacks to change aviation warning lights after a letter from the FAA is received
or a complete repair project involving a number of crews. It is still not unusual
to hear a company executive respond, “Oh, we don’t send our people up there—
we contract that out!” This means elevated tasks at a particular worksite can be
accomplished, provided the contractor’s employees are well trained, well equipped,
and guided by solid requirements in the bid document and contractor rulebook
to provide fall protection followed by the necessary site-specific training. This is
especially important to the owner because of third-party legal relationships, which
are not easily appreciated. Therefore, a workable system for establishing and
checking procedures and then observing for compliance is critical and may involve
a local safety consultant to review work if no qualified maintenance person or
safety professional is available.
Falls, caused by slipping or tripping, can lead to more serious elevated falls and
must be addressed (see Chapter 4).
Public fall exposure at elevation is presented primarily by stairs and a myriad of
railing designs, followed by ladders, roofs, and walking close to construction sites.
Tree stands pose a major fall threat to 30 million hunters, which is of particular
interest to employers, who expect their hunter- workers to show up on Mondays
during the hunting season.
Fall Protection from a Historical Perspective
“When one falls, it is not one’s foot that is to blame.”—Chinese proverb
For thousands of years, people have used ropes and various knots to help
move or secure objects against the forces of gravity. Bend knots were used to
gain a reliable hold, and hitch knots were used in moving a load by sliding along
another rope and, if necessary, gripping to lock the load in place. The practice of
people climbing ladders and/or being suspended on ropes and using these same
knots for positioning is primarily an outgrowth of the rigging trades. Some earlier
users would have been found on sailing ships, in church steeple construction and
maintenance, in mines, and in tree-trimming trades.
Ropes and some type of body belt, for restraint or work-positioning support,
were particularly useful during stormy seas and above the decks of ships. A similar
development of harness, rope, and knot usage originated more recently from cliff
and cave rescue, as well as from mountaineering techniques. In the middle 1800s,
Introduction to Fall Protection • 9

Collapse of Work Surfaces
Collapse of work surfaces is usually found on construction sites, scaffolds, and
roofs due to insufficiently unsupported surfaces and renovation projects, due to
floor-material degradation or towers and antennas and corrosion, for example.
Before a worker walks on a work surface, such as a commercial roof or metal
decking, an engineer should have periodically reviewed the condition of the
structure and deemed it fit for use (OSHA 1926.501(a)(2)). This review can be done
from aerial lifts or crane-suspended work platforms, for evaluation of ladders and
platforms. Alternatively, subfloors can be observed from the floor below. When in
doubt, avoid human access, or consider grating or plywood working surfaces for
temporary use.
Trips: Falls on the Same Level
A trip is defined as a loss of balance due to the foot (or leg) contacting an object,
or obstruction, when the attention is directed to the path ahead. A slight increase
or decrease in the walking surface of one-quarter inch (6.35 mm) is often sufficient
to cause a stumble (trip), resulting in loss of balance. On occasion, too much
friction between the foot or footwear and the walking surface also can cause a trip,
especially when moving from one type of surface to another. Unsecured throw
rugs or raised door thresholds, result in tripping hazards in the home can also
cause problems; seniors would do well to put favorite rugs on the wall instead of
the floor.
Broken sign stubs on sidewalks or other walking areas need to be dealt with
immediately because pedestrians cannot easily see these kinds of tripping hazards,
and a severe fall can occur. Especially troublesome are shoelaces that can catch on
the obstruction and fling the person headfirst into the ground or another object.
Shoelace loops from one shoe can catch on the other shoe’s lacing hooks, resulting
in an abrupt fall, with a likely head injury. Another common problem is stepping
on loose shoelaces from the other shoe, which can produce a stumble.
Stumbles
A stumble is the loss of contact with a surface while walking or stepping up or
down, which may or may not result in a fall. A forward stumble could be the result
of an unexpected change in elevation, as when stepping off from an unusually
high curb for example. Stumbles backward can result from a sudden change in
elevation, such as an unobserved roof blister, next to an unguarded roof edge.
This can produce an involuntary backwards stumble that could be catastrophic.
Housekeeping
Poor or inadequate housekeeping, such as blocked aisles, exposed cords, and
uneven rugs, mats, or runners, are a few conditions that often produce trips.
A poor physical layout can promote dangerous shortcuts. The emotional state

include transportation and public utilities, forestry, mining, agriculture, fishing,
wholesale and retail trades, and services.
In 2006, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that fatal work injuries
involving falls increased 5 percent in 2006, after a sharp decrease in 2005. The 827
fatal falls in 2006 was the highest total since 1992, when the fatality census began.
Fatal falls from roofs increased from 160 fatalities in 2005 to 184 in 2006, a rise of
15 percent. Falls from ladders (16%), scaffolds (11%) and roofs (23%), still account
for the majority of falls. Identifying fall hazards and deciding how best to protect
workers is the first step in reducing or eliminating fall hazards. BLS reported a
decrease in fall deaths during 2008 and 2009. In 2009, BLS data indicated that
the number of fatal falls was down to a total of 645. BLS further surmised that
the decrease in fall deaths might have been a reflection of the decline in overall
construction activity, as construction accidents typically account for over half of
all fatal falls (BLS 2011). The U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) lists falls as one
of the leading causes of traumatic occupational death, accounting for 8 percent
of all occupational fatalities from trauma (DOL/BLS 2010). Any time a worker
is at a height of 4 feet or more, the worker is at risk and needs to be protected.
Fall protection must be provided at 4 feet trigger height in general industry,
5 feet in maritime, and 6 feet, generally, in construction. However, regardless of
the fall distance, fall protection must be provided when working over dangerous
equipment and machinery and in aerial lifts.
Has Fall Protection Been Available to and Used by Elevated Fall Victims?
In a unique 1984 BLS study, “Injuries Resulting from Falls from Elevation,”
10 percent of fall victims surveyed had been provided with fall arrest systems;
however, more than 75 percent were not attached to a lifeline or structure. The
majority of these workers reported, that they were unwilling or unable to connect
their body support because they were moving around. A few stated that there was
no place to connect their equipment. Sixteen workers were using fall protection
equipment at the time of their elevated falls. For 10 of these workers, the fall
protection consisted of a belt, attached with a lanyard, yet four sustained back
injuries from the fall arrest. That small sample of work-related incidents clearly
indicated that too many workers in American industry are not only injured or
killed, falling from one level to another, but a substantial number of falls resulted
from a failure to properly use and attach the fall arrest equipment.
BLS statistics tell us that from 1992 to 1999, fatal falls accounted for 10–11% of
all fatal work injuries, increasing to 12–14% during 2000–2006 (DOL/BLS 2008).
This suggests strongly that similar usage failures, despite great strides in training,
regulations, standards, and equipment, remain. This problem is not isolated within
one industry or one work task. Either fall protection is still not being adequately
provided or the equipment that is provided is being used or applied improperly.
22 • Introduction

We can plan safety at heights, and we can train employees in better work
methods, but too many supervisors still leave the entire choice of work method
and safety provisions to the worker. “After all, he chose this line of work, and has
the job experience, so he should know best,” goes the reasoning, along with “I
can’t be with the worker, and do her job for her.”
Workers often play into this rationale by saying the boss said he will get me
anything I want for safety. While that is nice, the worker does not know what to
ask for, so the hazard exposures remain.
Too often, the necessary tools for safety have not been provided to the worker.
Tolerating fall hazards has become an unconsciously accepted practice many
managers develop early in their careers. The critical safety knowledge needed to
deal with heights safely is not inherent in the minds of most managers. It must be
learned. They unfortunately think that workers who fall were not careful enough
or simply were unlucky. “Poor Joe, what a shame,” is the refrain.
Prevention or Fall Arrest as a Means of Fall Protection?
Sometimes, exposure to a fall hazard cannot be practically prevented during access
to a work task or when at a work position, through such measures as floors, walls,
aerial lifts, bucket trucks, guardrails, perimeter cables, crane-suspended work
platforms (manbaskets), scaffolds, or planking. In these situations, personal fall
arrest equipment can be selected to control a fall or alternatively provide a reliable
means of escape when a controlled-descent feature is employed.
In general, personal protective equipment is designed as a backup safety system
for an individual during a work task. In the event of an emergency, the equipment
should function automatically to help protect the worker from harm. A personal-fall
protection system should, therefore, provide continuous and complete protection
without interfering with required task mobility. Continuous fall protection uses
one or more of the following means:
• Fall Prevention
Barriers, Covers
Guardrails
Perimeter Cables
Walls, Fences
Platforms, Buckets, Aerial Lifts
Scaffolds, Planking
• Fall Arrest
Safety Nets
Personal Fall Arrest Systems
Continuous or 100% fall protection means no gaps in fall protection coverage.
Many ask whether this can be done on an economical or practical basis. Properly
used, equipment can often provide the most protection for the least cost with a
certain level of potential exposure.

Overall, an audit (examples of numerous types are published) can be used to
assess the effectiveness of the fall protection program. It is an opportunity to see
if previously set objectives have been met and to determine what changes need to
be made.
Fall protection programs often flounder early in their implementation because
too many details are left unaddressed. An audit committee is a good way to point
out weaknesses and focus on removing blockages to progress.
A program audit encompasses organized, periodic testing to ensure that the
objectives of a fall protection program are met. Regular evaluation of the effectiveness
of the managed fall protection program is a critical component in eliminating and
controlling fall hazards. This involves a continuous process of building on program
strengths and correcting deficiencies. The evaluations should examine the program
to determine whether it has accomplished its objectives and whether they have been
achieved according to the written program.
Safety personnel from another plant typically perform these audits. Using
checklists, they ask questions pertaining to training records, work methods,
incident records, content of training, remediation, and work practices, with respect
to established fall protection and the planning for fall protection solutions in
upcoming projects.
Review of audit results should be conducted to point out the successes and also
the shortcomings flagged by the audit. The results should be published to show
workers and management their progress. These results can also be used to set new
goals, as a result of input from all exposed workers and their supervisors. Part of
continuous improvement includes regularly scheduled program reviews and drills,
such as rescue drills.
The program administrator should evaluate program effectiveness periodically—
at least every two years, when Authorized Persons or Competent Persons identify
deficiencies, or when there are incidents involving injuries, property damage, or
near misses.
The documented program evaluation shall identify, for each element: program
strengths, program deficiencies, and recommendations for improvement. A
documented plan of action shall then be developed to identify what changes will
be made, who is responsible for making each change, and when the change will be
completed.
Program evaluations shall be retained on file for at least five years, longer if
mandated by a legislative authority.
Return on Investment
In the author’s experience, a serious or fatal injury occurs at an average of every
five to ten years in companies where workers are regularly exposed to elevated fall
hazards. Although this number may seem low relative to other injuries, the severity
of fall incidents is usually very high and typically produces lifelong consequences.
The cost of instituting a comprehensive fall protection program is negligible in
comparison to the economic benefits an employer receives. Because the severity
of a single fall incident is so high, whatever the existing general insurance and

Evaluation Criteria
The program evaluation must contain: a review of the written policy statement and
its application in the workplace; a determination that duties and responsibilities
have been appropriately assigned; a determination that the training for the required
personnel is adequate to perform their duties and responsibilities; a review of
training programs to verify that fall protection training conforms to the current
ANSI or CSA Standard and any applicable regulations; a review of existing fall-
hazard survey reports to ensure that all fall-hazard exposures have been identified;
a review of all fall protection equipment and systems currently in use; a review
of anchorage systems; a review of the process for purchasing fall protection
equipment/systems to ensure such equipment/systems meet the requirements
of this standard; a review of the inspection, maintenance, storage, and care for
fall protection equipment; a review of the fall protection procedures and rescue
procedures; a review of insurance claims to identify procedures, workplace activities,
or equipment that might be improved; evaluations of Authorized Persons; a review
of rescue drills; a review of fall protection and prevention considerations for new
buildings, facilities, and equipment; and a review of incident investigations.
The program must be evaluated by the program administrator at periodic
intervals not to exceed two years. Additionally, the program must be evaluated
when workers, supervisors, or Competent Persons identify deficiencies or when
there are incidents involving injuries, property damage, or near misses.
The program evaluation must identify the strengths and deficiencies for each
element of the managed fall protection program, along with recommendations
for improvement. This evaluation must be documented. Consideration should be
given to a team approach when developing recommendations, specifically including
management and employee involvement.
A documented plan of action must be developed, identifying what changes will
be made, who is responsible for making each change, and when the change will be
completed.
Program evaluations must be retained on file for the length of time mandated
by the applicable legislative authority, but not less than five years.

injury. Falling has always been and will continue to be a safety issue with serious
consequences. Therefore, considerable efforts need to be invested in the planning
and implementation of our work to assure that employees are protected from fall
exposures.

not yet be practical. An example might be when a portable tripod with adequate
strength is used to anchor both of the lines because of the need to keep the lines
directly overhead and centered in the opening. If harnesses are used to lower a
worker through a narrow opening, the same D-ring may be used. Yet, when a
saddle belt/harness or boatswain’s chair is used, a separate full body harness is
required because most saddle belts are worn loosely for comfort and the wearer
may fall out if a fall occurs. A MacCollum Hazard Analysis Grid and fault-tree
analysis or failure-modes and effects analysis is required for such situations to help
select the correct equipment components.
Steel Erection
Many fall protection challenges exist for those who work in steel erection. Very
narrow working surfaces are constantly being created as skeletal steel is erected. For
those who connect the steel beams and supports, the work starts at the top level
of the structure. Therefore, anchorage points above foot level are often limited
or unavailable. OSHA 1926.760 sets the requirements for fall protection in steel
erection. Steel-erection trigger heights for fall protection at 15 feet for erectors,
and 30 feet for connectors were finalized by OSHA in January 2001. A controlled
decking zone (CDZ) may be established in an area of the structure of more than
15 feet and up to 30 feet above a lower level where the metal decking is being
initially installed, and forms a leading edge of a work area. Between 15 and 30 feet,
and above 30 feet connectors must have fall protection available and in place.
Fall Protection Safety Rules for Steel Erection
Some general rules for fall protection in steel erection follow:
• Do erect post systems and cables from waist height to overhead on beams or
girders at the ground or shake-out level to provide protection for predictable
routes. Use quick-release methods for the release of hoisting slings.
• Do plan the routes of travel up and around the structure and stick to them.
• Do check to see whether harnesses have abraded or cut webbing under
the buttocks from cooning (straddling) work methods and if so replace the
harnesses.
• Do not use “beamer” type anchorage devices on bar joists or open web steel
joists, because angle iron is too flexible and the device may twist off in a fall,
Reference 1926.757.
• Do not work connecting steel in unusually windy or wet weather conditions.
• Use approved work boots for use on specific walking surfaces—especially
wet or painted steel.
Introduction to Fall Protection • 327

Fall Protection Equipment
Hardware components, including rope and webbing, that can be attached
together to provide a fall protection system. Sometimes includes work-positioning
components of equipment to hold the body and attach to a structure.
Fall Protection Plan (FPP)
A written document that describes the job task and work-method procedures
for the purpose of eliminating or controlling elevated fall hazards foreseeably
encountered in the work and that may include a statement as to why it is necessary
for ensuring the safety of identified workers by eliminating or reducing foreseeable
fall hazards (OSHA, 1926.502(k)).
Fall Protection Program
An organized, site-specific, written document comprising a fall protection policy,
rules, and procedures for elimination and control of identified fall hazards.
Fall Restraint System
A device or devices including any necessary components, that prevents an
authorized person from reaching a fall hazard (ANSI Z359.0-2007).
Fault-Tree Analysis
A safety-system method of uncovering postulated, undesirable end-events and
examining the range of potential events that could lead to this condition. For
example, an undesirable event involving a fall arrest system would be that the user
falls to the ground. The method identifies how that might happen. After various
paths are identified, they can be evaluated for the probability of occurrence.
(Adapted from the System Safety Society definition.)
Fixed Anchorage
A stationary point of attachment for lanyards, lifelines, or devices that is capable
of supporting at least twice the maximum potential force in each fall protection
system that may be used. See also: Anchorage.
Force Factor
The ratio of the arresting force on a rigid, metal test weight to the arresting force
on a human body having the same weight, both falling under identical conditions.
Force Test
An OSHA test designed to measure the maximum arrest force in a fall protection
equipment system.
Free Fall
The act of falling before the personal fall arrest system begins to apply force to
arrest the fall (OSHA 1910.66, Appendix C and ANSI Z359.0-2007).
Free Fall Distance
The vertical displacement of the fall arrest attachment point on the employee’s
body belt or body harness between onset of the fall and just before the system

Preface to the Fourth Edition
The fall-protection revolution has begun! Maybe it was the harness rule in the
United States on January 1, 1998, when harnesses became a requirement and body
belts became illegal for fall arrest. It took only about a year for almost complete
compliance—not only in construction but also in general industry and other
industries. The word got around fast that suspension in a belt was dangerous.
So why is the number and rate of fatal falls still steadily going up? I think there are
two reasons: First, the proper structural anchorage point has not caught on widely
yet (beyond the standard issue of a harness and Y-lanyard). Second, the users of
fall-protection systems do not understand that these systems must be engineered
into the workplace and also maintained with strong, effective programs that
resemble FAA requirements for maintenance of commercial aircraft components.
The program administrator recommended in ANSI Z359.2 can help establish a
stronger role for the Qualified Person and more discipline for the Competent
Person. Advisory standards must begin to focus on incorporation of elements into
the building codes to provide designers with a set of requirements so new buildings
are not immediately in violation of OSHA requirements when the certificate of
occupancy or equivalent is provided.
The Competent Person can help prevent or repair damage that is caused by others
inadvertently and deal with innocent misuse. And as more sophisticated equipment
gets more widely used, there is the tendency to forego critical observations of
how the equipment is actually being used. Supervisors who fail to frequently
monitor work practices, inspect equipment, and check site conditions do so at the
risk of exposing workers to swing falls, cable cutting hazards, rope degradation
under acid conditions, edge hazards, corrosion of cable terminations, SRL pawl
sticking, ground or surface impacts, Y-lanyard deployment hazards, and snaphook
attachment hazards, just to name a few.
This book provides multiple solutions to eliminate fall hazards in more than one
trade or situation and tools to improve fall-hazard observations and documentation.
Recommendations herein for personal training for the exposed worker are vitally
important to reduce exposure to falls, but so too are the many recommendations
for designing out fall hazards and providing engineered anchorages for those who
must maintain buildings long after they are built.
As we march down the road of progress with improved equipment and systems and
standards, let us not forget the importance of the skill of recognizing fall hazards.
Certain exposures, even for a few milliseconds of duration, such as during transitions,
xii • Preface to the Fourth Edition

are potentially lethal and must be addressed by proper training. Even the best
harness with slack webbing adjustment controls and convenient buckle tightening
cannot make up for a poor application or excess fall exposure or nonattachment.
J. Nigel Ellis, Ph.D., PE, CSP, CPE
Introduction to Fall Protection • xiii

Are There Fall Hazards in Every Industry?
Nearly every industry, at some time, engages in work at elevation. The job could
range from the simple use of a 10-foot stepladder to change a light bulb to operating
a powered platform 185 feet up inside a boiler or climbing 200 feet up a flare-stack
ladder. A short, but unique, six-month Bureau of Labor Statistics study (1984)
of approximately 77 elevated-fall injuries showed a variety of industries were
involved. Although injuries in the construction industry were predominant in this
survey (41%), nearly one-fourth of the victims were employed by manufacturers.
Forty-four percent of the injured workers were craft workers, including carpenters
(10%) and mechanics/repairers (6%). A large portion, 24 percent, were working
as laborers, while 12 percent were employed as operators. Other victims included
clerical and sales workers, managers, and transport equipment operators. The
author has found that annually, over the past three decades, the relative numbers
change very little, and surveys may be unique such as this one.
Certain industries, of course, require substantial elevated work. For instance,
frequent elevated tasks associated with transmission and distribution operations in
the utility industry are significantly different from operations within a microchip
processing plant. For those industries, with frequent activity at elevation, the
probability of a fall is consequently higher. In some industries, such as trucking,
the access problems to tank trucks, flatbeds, and soft sides, have hardly begun to
be observed.
There are two types of elevated fall exposure:
1. During Work. Elevated work can be an integral part of a job or trade.
Scalers, for example, whose job it is to remove built-up residue from tanks,
digesters, or vessels, are often exposed to fall hazards, slipping, and chemicals
on an ongoing basis. Other examples, often associated with construction or
maintenance, include roofing, painting, sandblasting, pipe welding, masonry,
or bricklaying, and utility service work. Steel connectors also commonly
work at great elevation.
2. During Access or Exit. In other cases, exposure to a fall hazard occurs
simply while the worker is accessing an elevated workstation. Repair of a
valve, located on the upper tier of a chemical processing pipe rack, may
require that the worker use a fixed ladder 25 to 100 yards away, then walk
the pipe to the valve. Some trades, such as scaffold builders, provide a local
means of access. However, fall protection for these workers, during erection
and dismantling, should not be ignored. Temporary systems can be brought
to the site and removed by the contract scaffold company. Alternatively,
fall protection for access can be provided by the principal/owner and used
throughout the job by other employees.
Access to work areas can provide the greatest hazards, depending upon the
access method selected. Use of a rental van roof to paint signs on an automobile
dealership window is novel but raises questions. Use of a six-foot stepladder, next
to or within a few feet of a guardrail, raises the danger stakes. Running computer
8 • Introduction

lines for process control away from the reach of heavy-duty forklifts puts battery
replacement service 10 feet overhead next to a column. Planning and coordination
is a must for access for repeat visits and especially for single visits. Wiring for the
internet and telecommunications has made utility access a significant hazard above
almost every corridor when old wires are not replaced and new wires follow no
plan for their location.
Often, contractors are brought in to perform elevated work. It could be a
maintenance contract that requires the contractor to climb unprotected towers
and stacks to change aviation warning lights after a letter from the FAA is received
or a complete repair project involving a number of crews. It is still not unusual
to hear a company executive respond, “Oh, we don’t send our people up there—
we contract that out!” This means elevated tasks at a particular worksite can be
accomplished, provided the contractor’s employees are well trained, well equipped,
and guided by solid requirements in the bid document and contractor rulebook
to provide fall protection followed by the necessary site-specific training. This is
especially important to the owner because of third-party legal relationships, which
are not easily appreciated. Therefore, a workable system for establishing and
checking procedures and then observing for compliance is critical and may involve
a local safety consultant to review work if no qualified maintenance person or
safety professional is available.
Falls, caused by slipping or tripping, can lead to more serious elevated falls and
must be addressed (see Chapter 4).
Public fall exposure at elevation is presented primarily by stairs and a myriad of
railing designs, followed by ladders, roofs, and walking close to construction sites.
Tree stands pose a major fall threat to 30 million hunters, which is of particular
interest to employers, who expect their hunter- workers to show up on Mondays
during the hunting season.
Fall Protection from a Historical Perspective
“When one falls, it is not one’s foot that is to blame.”—Chinese proverb
For thousands of years, people have used ropes and various knots to help
move or secure objects against the forces of gravity. Bend knots were used to
gain a reliable hold, and hitch knots were used in moving a load by sliding along
another rope and, if necessary, gripping to lock the load in place. The practice of
people climbing ladders and/or being suspended on ropes and using these same
knots for positioning is primarily an outgrowth of the rigging trades. Some earlier
users would have been found on sailing ships, in church steeple construction and
maintenance, in mines, and in tree-trimming trades.
Ropes and some type of body belt, for restraint or work-positioning support,
were particularly useful during stormy seas and above the decks of ships. A similar
development of harness, rope, and knot usage originated more recently from cliff
and cave rescue, as well as from mountaineering techniques. In the middle 1800s,
Introduction to Fall Protection • 9

The proper understanding of fall protection results in a commitment to
elimination of fall hazards, and this begins by recognizing fall hazards without
considering the risk. Let the insurance industry worry about the risk. By taking any
route, other than elimination of the hazard altogether, we keep the hazard alive.
Eliminating Fall Hazards
Eliminating fall hazards means finding a way to avoid the necessity of exposure to
heights. This is the number one goal of fall protection. If a hazard is eliminated,
then workers are not put at risk. For example, building a roof truss framework,
fully or partially at ground level, and lifting it into place, is better than assembling
it in the air while standing on the framing.
It’s true that all hazards cannot be eliminated from every particular situation.
However, by addressing the known hazards, we can predict how most of them
can be eliminated or reasonably controlled before workers are exposed to them.
A simple checklist is often all that’s needed because it forces visualization of how
the work is supposed to be done when completed correctly.
Also, simple products that effectively eliminate many fall hazards are available
on the market today. Some examples follow:
• A telescoping duster to remove cobwebs in the office or home. Basically
a dust mop on an extendable pole: this product allows a person to clean
ceilings, skylights, and stairwells without the use of a ladder.
• A fruit harvester. This product consists of a specially designed fruit-picking
basket that clamps onto any long pole. It eliminates fall hazards for workers
harvesting fruit from trees.
• Gutter cleaning device. This product consists of a sprayer that attaches to
a garden hose. An attached, extendable pole lifts the device to gutter level.
When the device is activated, high-pressure water blasts and lifts leaves and
debris from gutters, while the worker remains on the ground.
• Tank truck loading and unloading devices. Tank trucks that can be
loaded and unloaded by workers standing at ground level and eliminate fall
exposures for workers who would otherwise climb to the top of the tank
truck or trailer (Figure 1.13). Work from the ground, by design, requires
proper engineering and order by buyer of this model, for example vapor
recovery systems.
Are Fall Hazards Obvious?
Isn’t it obvious to any person (who may someday sit on a jury) that height hazards
are a known, severe-injury producer, if not a reasonably certain-fatality producer?
Then why don’t employers address this hazard exposure, which can be reasonably
eliminated or controlled? Why is such a severe and foreseeable hazard too often
Introduction to Fall Protection • 29

Figure 1.15. Guarded platforms for work on train cars
or trailers.
Arresting Falls
Arresting falls is the end result of the proper use of fall arrest equipment, such
as safety nets and personal protective equipment (fall arresters), where there is
sufficient clearance from a lower level.
Applying Administrative Techniques
Administrative techniques are those procedures that deal with work methods and
sequence to reduce fall hazards, such as specific routing to a certain elevated work
area or the correct way to set up and install a ladder. Where edge fall hazards
occur, the use of warning lines set back from an edge are reasonable. Assembly
of a platform’s grating at ground level is better than asking ironworkers to do the
same thing in the air. Debatable methods include the “qualified climber” concept,
safety monitoring by each and every worker, close-to-roof edges, one-time-allowed
exposures for inspection or job estimation, warning signs, and just the plain old “Be
Careful” or “Watch your step” or “Don’t fall.” The qualified climber is an attempt
to rationalize training and frequency of climbing as fall deterrents. However, the
author believes this concept is convenient, but futile. Perhaps it should be renamed
the “lucky climber” concept.4 One mistake in a journeyman worker’s career is all it
takes to disprove this theory for that particular worker.
From this primary hierarchy of fall protection (Figure 1.16) arises another, the
access hierarchy, addressing work platforms and how workers reach them. In order
of desirability, they are:
1. Elimination of the need to access
2. Temporary platforms/stairs

Overall, an audit (examples of numerous types are published) can be used to
assess the effectiveness of the fall protection program. It is an opportunity to see
if previously set objectives have been met and to determine what changes need to
be made.
Fall protection programs often flounder early in their implementation because
too many details are left unaddressed. An audit committee is a good way to point
out weaknesses and focus on removing blockages to progress.
A program audit encompasses organized, periodic testing to ensure that the
objectives of a fall protection program are met. Regular evaluation of the effectiveness
of the managed fall protection program is a critical component in eliminating and
controlling fall hazards. This involves a continuous process of building on program
strengths and correcting deficiencies. The evaluations should examine the program
to determine whether it has accomplished its objectives and whether they have been
achieved according to the written program.
Safety personnel from another plant typically perform these audits. Using
checklists, they ask questions pertaining to training records, work methods,
incident records, content of training, remediation, and work practices, with respect
to established fall protection and the planning for fall protection solutions in
upcoming projects.
Review of audit results should be conducted to point out the successes and also
the shortcomings flagged by the audit. The results should be published to show
workers and management their progress. These results can also be used to set new
goals, as a result of input from all exposed workers and their supervisors. Part of
continuous improvement includes regularly scheduled program reviews and drills,
such as rescue drills.
The program administrator should evaluate program effectiveness periodically—
at least every two years, when Authorized Persons or Competent Persons identify
deficiencies, or when there are incidents involving injuries, property damage, or
near misses.
The documented program evaluation shall identify, for each element: program
strengths, program deficiencies, and recommendations for improvement. A
documented plan of action shall then be developed to identify what changes will
be made, who is responsible for making each change, and when the change will be
completed.
Program evaluations shall be retained on file for at least five years, longer if
mandated by a legislative authority.

five to ten years in companies where workers are regularly exposed to elevated fall
hazards. Although this number may seem low relative to other injuries, the severity
of fall incidents is usually very high and typically produces lifelong consequences.

comparison to the economic benefits an employer receives. Because the severity

Preface to the Fourth Edition
The fall-protection revolution has begun! Maybe it was the harness rule in the
United States on January 1, 1998, when harnesses became a requirement and body
belts became illegal for fall arrest. It took only about a year for almost complete
compliance—not only in construction but also in general industry and other
industries. The word got around fast that suspension in a belt was dangerous.
So why is the number and rate of fatal falls still steadily going up? I think there are
two reasons: First, the proper structural anchorage point has not caught on widely
yet (beyond the standard issue of a harness and Y-lanyard). Second, the users of
fall-protection systems do not understand that these systems must be engineered
into the workplace and also maintained with strong, effective programs that
resemble FAA requirements for maintenance of commercial aircraft components.
The program administrator recommended in ANSI Z359.2 can help establish a
stronger role for the Qualified Person and more discipline for the Competent
Person. Advisory standards must begin to focus on incorporation of elements into
the building codes to provide designers with a set of requirements so new buildings
are not immediately in violation of OSHA requirements when the certificate of
occupancy or equivalent is provided.
The Competent Person can help prevent or repair damage that is caused by others
inadvertently and deal with innocent misuse. And as more sophisticated equipment
gets more widely used, there is the tendency to forego critical observations of
how the equipment is actually being used. Supervisors who fail to frequently
monitor work practices, inspect equipment, and check site conditions do so at the
risk of exposing workers to swing falls, cable cutting hazards, rope degradation
under acid conditions, edge hazards, corrosion of cable terminations, SRL pawl
sticking, ground or surface impacts, Y-lanyard deployment hazards, and snaphook
attachment hazards, just to name a few.
This book provides multiple solutions to eliminate fall hazards in more than one
trade or situation and tools to improve fall-hazard observations and documentation.
Recommendations herein for personal training for the exposed worker are vitally
important to reduce exposure to falls, but so too are the many recommendations
for designing out fall hazards and providing engineered anchorages for those who
must maintain buildings long after they are built.
As we march down the road of progress with improved equipment and systems and
standards, let us not forget the importance of the skill of recognizing fall hazards.

For proper development of the fall protection team, Qualified Persons initially
must become Competent Persons. A Qualified Person is one who, by possession
of a recognized degree, certificate, professional standing, or extensive knowledge,
training, and experience, has successfully demonstrated their ability to (re)solve
problems relating to the site-specific work to be done. [This is a paraphrase of
OSHA 1926.32(m).] ANSI Z359.0 further defines a Qualified Person as “a person
with a recognized degree or professional certificate and with extensive knowledge,
training, and experience in the fall protection and rescue field who is capable of
designing, analyzing, evaluating, and specifying fall protection and rescue systems.”
There may be several Qualified Persons appointed for a particular project.
The Qualified Person serves as an interface between the work structure and the
worker. For example, the Qualified Person works with permanent and temporary
anchorages and any unusual situations that arise which need engineering expertise.
While this Qualified Person may often be an engineer with a structural and/or
mechanical specialty, OSHA does not require an engineer to perform this duty;
however, many jurisdictions require that individuals who design or evaluate physical
structures be registered with the jurisdiction as a professional engineer. Remember
the words in the definition above: “extensive knowledge, training and experience.”
Figure 9.3 relates safety engineering to other engineering specialties. Safety
Engineering covers all fields where individuals are exposed to hazards. Hazards are
recognized and designs implemented to eliminate recognized hazards.
The author believes that Qualified Persons in fall protection should be
specialists in Safety Engineering. Safety Engineering is a broad discipline that
includes aspects of all others forms of engineering. For example, the engineer
who designs an airplane must consider the proper design of work platforms
to assemble or service the aircraft. Likewise, a chemical engineer may have to
consider weather or chemical-resistant lifeline systems for workers who must
negotiate pipe racks in a chemical plant. Qualified Persons in fall protection
should be specialists in safety engineering. Safety engineering is a discipline
that draws on knowledge from many engineering principles and practices.

engineer who manages a chemical plant may have to consider whether to design in

When an error probability level of 3 or 4 is multiplied by an error severity level
of 3 or 4, the result can be a risk level exceeding 13 points, meaning unacceptable.
If the risk level is over 9 points, it certainly indicates a serious problem. Elevated
fall hazards measured by either a lack of previous accident experience or risk level
prior to any fall incident—probability and/or severity—must be addressed.
Note that although a similar appraisal of risk is made by OSHA compliance
officers, the trend in the United States is to emphasize the severity rating (error
impact) as much more important than the modifying frequency rate (error
probability). The error impact for falls must always be very high. Therefore, any
foreseeable exposure to a fall hazard needs to be addressed urgently in planning.
The chance of making an error that results in an elevated fall is usually very
low for those frequently exposed to height hazards, but fall rates are quite high
for those where climbing and working in high places is often incidental to their
occupations (e.g., sheet metal workers, painters, and mechanics) (AFISC 1978).
Interestingly, the average age of the 210 ironworkers who lost their lives between
1981 and 1985 was 40 (The Ironworker 1986). This indicates greater complacency
or error frequency as experience grows among members of this group, who are
normally accustomed to working at heights. Whether a worker is experienced with
heights or not, that worker only has to make one major mistake in his or her career
for a life to be permanently changed.
Errors by skilled workers in trades are often related to unusual conditions,
which can combine to surprise a normally careful worker’s lack of awareness
in a particular situation. One example is a carpenter who was assisting in attaching
slings to remove a 10-foot column form at the edge of a concrete hotel/
condominium complex 30 stories up. While signaling the tower crane operator to
lift, he stepped back off the 6-inch slab and fell between the unguarded post
tensioning cables, left exposed because the tensioner had failed. He could not hold
onto the greased cables long enough to be helped and fell to the ground. In another
example, ironworkers may need to complete a lift at the end of the day and may
take shortcuts. The sure-footed connector, who usually coons the beam, may walk
or run on top of the girder to catch the steel instead and trip on a bolt placed on a
beam. A gust of wind may catch him unaware. Also, epoxy-painted steel, dew
patches in the shade, ice, or dust all appear at various times of the day throughout
the year to catch an unwary ironworker off guard. Tag lines to control the swing
of a load may also snag a worker, who cannot remove his hand from a webbing
loop (sling), and drag him off the structure. Worse consequences occur if a
helicopter lift encounters a wind shift and the worker is dragged over the stub
column or is still attached to the tower leg with his harness and lanyard. The best
practice is to keep taglines straight with no loops.
According to a unique 1981–85 study, ironworkers’ accidents usually occur
just before noon, just after lunch, or just before quitting time, when a worker’s
personal guard is lower (The Ironworker 1986). The air force collected similar
statistics in a 1970–77 study (AFISC). These human fallibilities point to the need
for more disciplined work procedures and workplaces that are designed to be more
error-tolerant.

Introduction to Fall Protection • xiii

Are There Fall Hazards in Every Industry?
Nearly every industry, at some time, engages in work at elevation. The job could
range from the simple use of a 10-foot stepladder to change a light bulb to operating
a powered platform 185 feet up inside a boiler or climbing 200 feet up a flare-stack
ladder. A short, but unique, six-month Bureau of Labor Statistics study (1984)
of approximately 77 elevated-fall injuries showed a variety of industries were
involved. Although injuries in the construction industry were predominant in this
survey (41%), nearly one-fourth of the victims were employed by manufacturers.
Forty-four percent of the injured workers were craft workers, including carpenters
(10%) and mechanics/repairers (6%). A large portion, 24 percent, were working
as laborers, while 12 percent were employed as operators. Other victims included
clerical and sales workers, managers, and transport equipment operators. The
author has found that annually, over the past three decades, the relative numbers
change very little, and surveys may be unique such as this one.
Certain industries, of course, require substantial elevated work. For instance,
frequent elevated tasks associated with transmission and distribution operations in
the utility industry are significantly different from operations within a microchip
processing plant. For those industries, with frequent activity at elevation, the
probability of a fall is consequently higher. In some industries, such as trucking,
the access problems to tank trucks, flatbeds, and soft sides, have hardly begun to
be observed.
There are two types of elevated fall exposure:
1. During Work. Elevated work can be an integral part of a job or trade.
Scalers, for example, whose job it is to remove built-up residue from tanks,
digesters, or vessels, are often exposed to fall hazards, slipping, and chemicals
on an ongoing basis. Other examples, often associated with construction or
maintenance, include roofing, painting, sandblasting, pipe welding, masonry,
or bricklaying, and utility service work. Steel connectors also commonly
work at great elevation.
2. During Access or Exit. In other cases, exposure to a fall hazard occurs
simply while the worker is accessing an elevated workstation. Repair of a
valve, located on the upper tier of a chemical processing pipe rack, may
require that the worker use a fixed ladder 25 to 100 yards away, then walk
the pipe to the valve. Some trades, such as scaffold builders, provide a local
means of access. However, fall protection for these workers, during erection
and dismantling, should not be ignored. Temporary systems can be brought
to the site and removed by the contract scaffold company. Alternatively,
fall protection for access can be provided by the principal/owner and used
throughout the job by other employees.
Access to work areas can provide the greatest hazards, depending upon the
access method selected. Use of a rental van roof to paint signs on an automobile
dealership window is novel but raises questions. Use of a six-foot stepladder, next
to or within a few feet of a guardrail, raises the danger stakes. Running computer
8 • Introduction

lines for process control away from the reach of heavy-duty forklifts puts battery
replacement service 10 feet overhead next to a column. Planning and coordination
is a must for access for repeat visits and especially for single visits. Wiring for the
internet and telecommunications has made utility access a significant hazard above
almost every corridor when old wires are not replaced and new wires follow no
plan for their location.
Often, contractors are brought in to perform elevated work. It could be a
maintenance contract that requires the contractor to climb unprotected towers
and stacks to change aviation warning lights after a letter from the FAA is received
or a complete repair project involving a number of crews. It is still not unusual
to hear a company executive respond, “Oh, we don’t send our people up there—
we contract that out!” This means elevated tasks at a particular worksite can be
accomplished, provided the contractor’s employees are well trained, well equipped,
and guided by solid requirements in the bid document and contractor rulebook
to provide fall protection followed by the necessary site-specific training. This is
especially important to the owner because of third-party legal relationships, which
are not easily appreciated. Therefore, a workable system for establishing and
checking procedures and then observing for compliance is critical and may involve
a local safety consultant to review work if no qualified maintenance person or
safety professional is available.
Falls, caused by slipping or tripping, can lead to more serious elevated falls and
must be addressed (see Chapter 4).
Public fall exposure at elevation is presented primarily by stairs and a myriad of
railing designs, followed by ladders, roofs, and walking close to construction sites.
Tree stands pose a major fall threat to 30 million hunters, which is of particular
interest to employers, who expect their hunter- workers to show up on Mondays
during the hunting season.
Fall Protection from a Historical Perspective
“When one falls, it is not one’s foot that is to blame.”—Chinese proverb
For thousands of years, people have used ropes and various knots to help
move or secure objects against the forces of gravity. Bend knots were used to
gain a reliable hold, and hitch knots were used in moving a load by sliding along
another rope and, if necessary, gripping to lock the load in place. The practice of
people climbing ladders and/or being suspended on ropes and using these same
knots for positioning is primarily an outgrowth of the rigging trades. Some earlier
users would have been found on sailing ships, in church steeple construction and
maintenance, in mines, and in tree-trimming trades.
Ropes and some type of body belt, for restraint or work-positioning support,
were particularly useful during stormy seas and above the decks of ships. A similar
development of harness, rope, and knot usage originated more recently from cliff

The proper understanding of fall protection results in a commitment to
elimination of fall hazards, and this begins by recognizing fall hazards without
considering the risk. Let the insurance industry worry about the risk. By taking any
route, other than elimination of the hazard altogether, we keep the hazard alive.
Eliminating Fall Hazards
Eliminating fall hazards means finding a way to avoid the necessity of exposure to
heights. This is the number one goal of fall protection. If a hazard is eliminated,
then workers are not put at risk. For example, building a roof truss framework,
fully or partially at ground level, and lifting it into place, is better than assembling
it in the air while standing on the framing.
It’s true that all hazards cannot be eliminated from every particular situation.
However, by addressing the known hazards, we can predict how most of them
can be eliminated or reasonably controlled before workers are exposed to them.
A simple checklist is often all that’s needed because it forces visualization of how
the work is supposed to be done when completed correctly.
Also, simple products that effectively eliminate many fall hazards are available
on the market today. Some examples follow:
• A telescoping duster to remove cobwebs in the office or home. Basically
a dust mop on an extendable pole: this product allows a person to clean
ceilings, skylights, and stairwells without the use of a ladder.
• A fruit harvester. This product consists of a specially designed fruit-picking
basket that clamps onto any long pole. It eliminates fall hazards for workers
harvesting fruit from trees.
• Gutter cleaning device. This product consists of a sprayer that attaches to
a garden hose. An attached, extendable pole lifts the device to gutter level.
When the device is activated, high-pressure water blasts and lifts leaves and
debris from gutters, while the worker remains on the ground.
• Tank truck loading and unloading devices. Tank trucks that can be
loaded and unloaded by workers standing at ground level and eliminate fall
exposures for workers who would otherwise climb to the top of the tank
truck or trailer (Figure 1.13). Work from the ground, by design, requires
proper engineering and order by buyer of this model, for example vapor
recovery systems.
Are Fall Hazards Obvious?
Isn’t it obvious to any person (who may someday sit on a jury) that height hazards
are a known, severe-injury producer, if not a reasonably certain-fatality producer?
Then why don’t employers address this hazard exposure, which can be reasonably
eliminated or controlled? Why is such a severe and foreseeable hazard too often

Arresting Falls
Arresting falls is the end result of the proper use of fall arrest equipment, such
as safety nets and personal protective equipment (fall arresters), where there is
sufficient clearance from a lower level.
Applying Administrative Techniques
Administrative techniques are those procedures that deal with work methods and
sequence to reduce fall hazards, such as specific routing to a certain elevated work
area or the correct way to set up and install a ladder. Where edge fall hazards
occur, the use of warning lines set back from an edge are reasonable. Assembly
of a platform’s grating at ground level is better than asking ironworkers to do the
same thing in the air. Debatable methods include the “qualified climber” concept,
safety monitoring by each and every worker, close-to-roof edges, one-time-allowed
exposures for inspection or job estimation, warning signs, and just the plain old “Be
Careful” or “Watch your step” or “Don’t fall.” The qualified climber is an attempt
to rationalize training and frequency of climbing as fall deterrents. However, the
author believes this concept is convenient, but futile. Perhaps it should be renamed
the “lucky climber” concept.4 One mistake in a journeyman worker’s career is all it
takes to disprove this theory for that particular worker.
From this primary hierarchy of fall protection (Figure 1.16) arises another, the
access hierarchy, addressing work platforms and how workers reach them. In order
of desirability, they are:

Large-scale spills from oil-storage tanks are typically contained in dikes. Small spills

that cannot easily be seen by others.

resulting slippery areas from accumulated water or ice. A new door with seals or a

• Catch points on the scaffold for the lifeline. Be careful to eliminate nip

careful to avoid the grab catching on a railing during a descent and putting
explosive dynamic stress on the line, which could spring dangerously into

• Attachment to anchorages if tie-backs are not available. Web or
steel slings should be attached around a substantial structure capable of
supporting 6,000 lbs. Steel snaphooks with locking design should be used to
link the lifeline to the sling. Lifelines should be terminated in a splice. Have
various lengths of lifelines available for buildings of different heights.
• Warnings and Signage. Safety cones should be used with caution tape
between them, and a sign should be posted indicating work activity in the
area and to keep out. This applies at ground level and on a roof to warn other
contractor personnel. Note: Taping off an area or providing signage should
never alone be considered fall protection. The fall protection hierarchy of
controls should always be considered.
• Special Applications. Steel-cable lifeline devices, including retracting steel
or Kevlar lifelines, are an alternative in heat-producing applications that
are protected from grounding by a section of split hose and are useful for
welding work.
The Connecting Hardware
The choice of snaphooks to link rope-grab components is a vital safety matter.
Only instructions from the manufacturer of the rope grab should be followed to
ensure the hardware is compatible. No other snaphooks should be used to avoid
potential roll-out or burst-out. Other parts of this book address the problems of
mixing and matching and misuse. All snaphooks should be of self-locking design,
maintained in optimum operating condition, and discarded if they are jammed or
damaged.
If a manufacturer’s snaphook instructions for use and inspection are not crystal
clear, a new manufacturer should be sought.
The Testing
When purchasing a rope-grab system or retracting lifeline, an operator should ask
for documentation that the system meets OSHA 1910.66 or 1926, Subpart M, test
requirements, and that it meets the strict force limits imposed by the standard.
The Training
The distributor or manufacturer may additionally be able to provide limited or
periodic training for operators. Training is discussed in detail in Chapter 11.

cleaning, bridge inspection, and tank entry often use this type of work-

Homemade work-positioning devices built from hooks, chains, slings, and
belt components are a scourge in the wall form, telecommunications, and other
industries. They are problematic because they have no compatibility, but mainly

Descent-Control Devices
Descent-control devices incorporate a place for work tools, a means of descent
with variable speed, and a manual method of control. Boatswain’s chairs are
typically used with descent-control devices when persons are working on vertical
faces of structures. The short-time use of these devices can make web seats on
harnesses acceptable, but they are very uncomfortable. They may be useful only
for an emergency or for egress after a fall has occurred.
The use of an overspeed-control feature is a critical development for these
devices when an approved descent line is used. This overspeed-control feature
does not require manual control of the rate of decent on the lifeline. Additionally,
because some of these descent-control devices are so easy to use, they are more
readily accepted by workers, which obviously leads to a safer work environment.
All workers using descent devices, such as for descent into hazardous areas,
should also receive instruction on their safe use.
Window cleaning and building maintenance are examples of primary
applications for friction devices designed as variable-speed descent devices, but
not for controlled descent.
Descent devices installed at roof level may be used over parapets if an acceptable
access means is provided. If little or no parapet exists, the cable or rope loadline
will lie across the edge of the structure as the descent progresses. This hazard

Introduction
Any company that has employees who are potentially exposed to fall hazards
should have a written comprehensive managed fall protection program. This
program is important because it establishes guidelines and requirements to protect
those employees and contractors who are exposed to potential falls while working
at elevation. The elements of a managed fall protection program are detailed in
this chapter and when properly implemented will give management and employees
the tools they need to prevent fall incidents, injuries and fatalities. The questions in
Table 9.1 can help you assess your fall protection program.
A managed fall protection program should not be confused with a “Fall
Protection Plan” as defined by OSHA construction standards (1926.502(k)
and Subpart M Appendix E. A fall protection plan is prepared and followed by
employers engaged in leading-edge work, precast concrete construction work, and
residential construction work who can demonstrate that it is infeasible or creates
a greater hazard to use conventional fall protection systems. A fall protection
program is a company-specific document detailing procedures for identifying and
addressing fall hazards in the workplace. Fall protection programs may be prepared
for general industry or construction applications or both.
In 2007, ANSI issued Minimum Requirements for a Comprehensive Managed Fall
Protection Program (Z359.2-2007) which calls for a program that addresses fall hazards
using the hierarchy of controls (as described in Chapter 3) including: elimination;
installation of passive fall protection measures; use of fall restraint; use of fall
arrest; and, as a last resort, use of administrative controls. At the time of printing,
there is no comparable consensus standard for construction activities. The ANSI
Standard for Fall Protection in Construction (A10.32) has not yet been updated to
include recommendations for comprehensive managed fall protection programs
for construction activities. However, most of the requirements of Z359.2 can be
applied to construction work—and the author recommends that this guidance be
followed by construction companies when preparing their fall protection programs
until an applicable construction standard is published.
The term comprehensive in the title of the standard indicates that the program
must clearly call for the identification, evaluation, and elimination (or control) of
fall hazards through planning; ensure proper training of personnel; ensure proper
installation and use of fall protection and rescue equipment; and provide for
implementation of safe fall protection and rescue procedures.
The term managed implies that program development and implementation is not
a one-time procedure, but an ongoing process. Endorsement of the employer’s fall
protection program by company management is emphasized.
ANSI Z359.2 provides the following six steps to a Managed Fall Protection
Program:
1. Commitment from Senior Management including policy statement
2. Appointment and training of steering committees

Elimination and Control of Fall Hazards
Determining Appropriate Fall-Hazard Control Measures
Once an elevated fall hazard has been analyzed, an appropriate control measure
must be selected. Use of the fall protection hierarchy of controls is essential to
choosing the method of fall protection to be used. The most effective controls
of health and safety hazards are those which are integrated or designed into the
process, such as engineering controls and passive methods of fall protection. The
least effective controls involve personal protective equipment and procedures that
merely acknowledge the hazard and do nothing to eliminate it.
Elimination
Where fall-hazard exposure is predicted, careful planning can eliminate the bulk of
the exposure. For example, if an operator must access a valve that is 30 feet above
the ground, this hazard can be eliminated by either repiping the line so the valve
is at ground level or by putting a motorized control valve in the line that allow the
operator to push a button while standing safely on the ground. A chain-operated
valve may also be an alternative control in the field of elimination but has been
known to lasso bicyclists.
Prevention
Preventive measures typically involve the installation of floors, walls, nets, or
fixed platforms and walking surfaces with the appropriate guardrails, midrails,
and toe boards. These measures usually consist of permanent passive systems,
but all require engineering and installation efforts. Scaffolding with temporary
floors and appropriate guarding may be suitable; however, the fall exposure during
erection and dismantling must be addressed. Another prevention method is to
deny personnel access to a location where they may be exposed to a fall hazard,
usually by thoughtful placement of deck pans at most 19" apart. Restricted access
can be achieved through the use of chains, barricades, tape, or signs. For example,
tape or cables can be used to warn workers to keep away from the edge of a roof
or skylight but only on a temporary basis. The hazard will still remain.
As mentioned above with regard to scaffold erection and dismantling,
permanent preventive measures almost always involve fall-hazard exposure during
the installation process. Therefore, personal protective equipment may be needed
to control a fall during the installation or dismantling/demolition process. This
often can be achieved with overhead or portable anchorage points. A secondary
method is the use of the scaffold members as part of an engineered fall arrest

The rescue plan should be supplemented by detailed rescue procedures that
provide a step-by-description of the specific manner in which rescue at each
location is to be accomplished. As discussed above, whenever personal fall arrest
systems are used, there must be a rescue plan in place to ensure that the victim can
self-rescue or be promptly rescued in the event that a fall occurs.
A checklist for emergency response after a fall is included in Figure 12.3.
Figure 12.4 presents a sample rescue plan.
RespondingtoanEmergency—A checklist for rescuing a suspended worker
Whenanemergencyoccurs
• If a suspended worker can’t perform a self-rescue, call the on-site emergency-response team and
get the appropriate rescue equipment.
• First responders should clear a path to the victim. Others should direct emergency personnel to
the scene.
• Prohibit all nonessential personnel from the rescue scene.
• Talk to the worker and try to determine the worker’s condition.
• If the worker is accessible, provide comfort and check vital signs. If necessary, administer CPR
and attempt to stop bleeding.
• If the worker’s injuries are minor, proceed with the rescue. Only trained responders should
attempt a technical rescue.
• If the worker has severe injuries, contact emergency medical responders. Remember, 911
responders may not be able to accomplish prompt rescues.
Afteranyemergency
• Report fatalities and catastrophes to the appropriate agency within eight hours. Report injuries
requiring overnight hospitalization and medical treatment other than first aid to the appropriate
agency within twenty-four hours.
• Document what went wrong, step by step.
• Identify all equipment that may have contributed to the emergency. Let a Qualified Person—one
who has the knowledge, the experience, and the demonstrated ability to resolve fall protection
and rescue problems—examine the equipment. If the equipment was damaged, repair or replace
it. If the equipment contributed to the emergency, determine why and how.
• Determine what caused the emergency. Be as specific as possible. Include dates, times,
environmental conditions, work processes, and persons involved.
• Review the emergency-response plan. Determine what procedures should be added or changed
to prevent similar emergencies. Revise the plan accordingly.

The U.S. Department of Labor’s proposed standard preamble to the 1910.129

These guidelines incorporate new fall protection technology for increased

often contract with outside businesses for their repair and construction work, they
are well aware of the OSHA 1926.500 regulations, and many have made these more

Standards Around the World: Status Relative to the United States
The United States still trails behind many foreign countries relative to the requirements
of its standards and the degree of fall protection offered to many workers.
The Canadian Ministry of Labour administers Canada’s national fall protection
regulations. Since its initial publication in 1978, the Canadian Standards Association
(CSA) guidelines continue to advance on the issue of fall arrest equipment
component standards.
France, Britain, Sweden, Finland, Germany, Japan, and Canada have been
considerably more advanced in this area of safety standards. For example, in 1978,
France banned the use of a body belt to meet its national fall arrest requirements.
A year later, Britain followed suit by limiting the use of body belts to where free
falls are less than 2 feet.

concerning what can cause injury. OSHA’s General Industry Process Safety
Regulations (29 CFR 1910.119) and automobile seat-belt laws provide excellent
precedents for workers regarding the need for effective safety procedures and
equipment.
The primary rule is to apply fall protection when the height hazard exceeds a
reasonable figure of a few feet—or at any height, if continued exposure is not
preventable. The responsibility of the equipment vendor to educate an end user
is limited by the extent that the customer (i.e., the end user’s employer) has a
bona fide no-fall policy rather than a tie-off policy, which is common among
employers. It also depends upon the manufacturer’s instructions, labeling, and
product literature, and whether the employer and employees follow these items for
reasonably foreseeable or permitted uses. Workers must be provided with, and be
required to read and understand, product instructions and labeling on fall arrest
equipment.
A book of instructions for safety products should be kept in the same
location as the Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) for collective ease
of access.
How Should Responsibility Flow?
The knowledgeable owner and/or controlling contractor must set safety policy
that permits the safety department to make reasonable rules on fall protection that
must be followed in work practice. Construction managers must be required to
enforce the safety rules as part of their job requirements. It is the chief operating
officer’s job to ensure that this is done in a formal way.
Thus, the employer sets standards and enforces them through the procedures
for his or her own employees. If the employer does not set and enforce standards
because of unfamiliarity with construction or maintenance practices, then the
obligation falls to the architect/engineer, consulting engineer, and/or general
contractor. But the owner must officially delegate the responsibility to the
contractor or engineering firm and monitor the contractor’s implementation
effectiveness. Finally, the owner must verify that the engineering firm/architect
accepts this responsibility (Philo and Steinberg 1979).
The unknowledgeable owner (one with no or limited knowledge of hazards) must
rely on a competent architect and general contractor for price and completion and
for prevention of accidents and death to anyone on the job. The unknowledgeable
owner’s representative may have a nondelegable duty to ensure fall protection.
Both the architect’s duty and the general contractor’s duty is to formally warn
the unknowledgeable owner about elevated fall hazards and the reasonable cost of
controlling them. This includes dangers of falling through unprotected skylights
with nominal impact. Recent evidence shows that construction projects can benefit
from an average of 35 percent bare labor savings when a 100 percent fall policy is
adopted and applied.

Safety Monitors
Safety monitors are appointed individuals on a roof whose job is to ensure that
trained workers have notice when stepping too close (within 6 feet) to a dangerous
edge. A safety monitor is not to have any other collateral duties while performing
their safety monitoring duties. OSHA addresses training requirements for both the
worker and the safety monitor (OSHA 1926.502(h)). Normally, for roofs 50 feet or
less, a safety monitor can be used and there is no requirement for a warning line,
although one should be used to mark a distance 6 feet from an edge to help the
monitor focus his or her attention (OSHA 1926.502(h)).
Safety monitors can usually watch up to 8 workers. When the monitor goes
closer than 6 feet to an edge, another safety monitor is appointed to be on duty.
Safety monitors are not permitted on roofs with greater than 4 in 12 slope or that
have equipment, such as a boiling tar bucket that could obscure vision or be too
noisy to allow communication. All workers must stay within the monitor’s line of
sight; all have to be able to hear the oral warnings of the monitor so they can react
immediately (OSHA 1926.502(h)). Often workers will step forward or backward
toward an edge at up to 4 or 5 feet per second, so the position of each worker has
to be carefully observed.
It is common for a safety monitor to wear a bright vest or other distinctive
clothing to broadcast his or her role as a monitor. In fact, today, hard-hat high-
visibility safety covers are available as well as high-visibility vests. The biggest
danger a monitor faces is being distracted so that persons within 6 feet of a fall
hazard are not cautioned precisely at the moment of impending hazard. It is at
these moments that the safety-monitor program fails, and management must
depend upon barriers, warning lines, and fall arrest systems properly applied.
It is always preferable to have anchorage installed in roofing systems to provide
a positive means of fall protection. Workers attaching to anchorage points on
existing roofs should be aware of rust or rot issues that might compromise the
integrity of the anchorage point. Manufacturers have made mobile anchor points
trailers for lifting onto a roof which claw into the roof surface upon a fall occurring
and are increasingly popular among the roofing trade for quick and convenient
hook up. In the author’s experience, the general feeling among roofers is that safety
monitors are unreliable after 20 years of use under OSHA regulation. Positive
anchored fall protection is the best way to protect roofing workers.

fall protection during roofing activities.
