lightweight, low-cost designs. However, it is potentially dangerous to consider
equipment components that have not been designed into an industrial fall
equipment system and certified as such by the supplier. It’s a trap for the unwary.
Consider the following.
The buyer and user of nearly all mountaineering equipment hardware, harnesses,
and rope is the same person. The responsibility for equipment use is clearly the
user’s, and this equipment is for a sports activity, not a work occupation. Hence,
a snap with no safety lock or manual screw lock may be a reasonable design for
mountaineering methods of use.
In industry, however, workers must not use fall arrest equipment unless they have
been trained, and the responsibility for training, equipment use, and maintenance
rests with the individual or individuals authorizing the use of fall arrest equipment.
Furthermore, equipment abuse, lack of maintenance, and especially the potential
for dirty conditions and chemical contamination in industrial settings are not
considerations in mountaineering-equipment design.
The best approach here is to stay away from sports equipment and to request
only industrial-grade models, certified to meet OSHA requirements and ANSI
standards. Note: One or two manufacturers have made the transition between
sports use and industrial use; user discretion is advised
Hazard: Electrical
Electric utilities need to provide standards for the use of fall arrest equipment,
including the following issues.
• Live-line transmission and distribution work calls for fall protection
and fall arrest equipment systems to meet electrical resistance
requirements, similar to those of hand, arm, foot, and climbing gear.
254 • Active Fall Protection Systems

7. A 20-foot scaffold is to be built on the outside of a vessel up to a manway opening 45 feet above the
ground. After thorough training, what fall protection would you expect to see planned for each worker
during erection?
a. lanyard and harness
b. two lanyards, or a Y-lanyard, and harness
c. retractable SRL and harness
d. horizontal lifelines, rope grab, and harness
8. In a heavily trussed production building, a roof project involves taking out a concrete roof (Transite
panels) that has a product history of not supporting human weight reliably as it has aged. The workers
have caulked translucent panels (skylights) regularly and have been told to walk only on the purlins to
which the panels are attached (they walk the screw-line). Your horizontal lifeline solution is installed, but
workers are afraid that they will swing back through the opening into the building’s ceiling obstructions.
What should you do?
a. Provide a cover for the opening before it is created.
b. Use a second horizontal lifeline attached to each person to prevent swing hazards.
c. Roof the building over again with a reliable sealer.
d. Make the roof off-limits.
9. Your field people are calling to have you approve a lifeline device for residential roofing that the OSHA
compliance officer called “inadequate for fall arrest.” The manufacturer of the device states in his
literature that it can be used either for work positioning or fall arrest as a “universal” fall protection
device. You go see and apply which one of the following as a key test?
a. Lean on the line to determine whether balance can be reasonably maintained.
b. Check whether the labeling references OSHA/ANSI standards.
c. Check if the harness is designed for fall arrest.
d. Confirm that a work-positioning device must also be supported by a fall arrest device.
10. Your new annual report shows several striking photographs of the public works construction projects
you have completed in the past year as safety manager. The board is immensely proud to include these,
but an outside safety-trained director points out that almost every photo shows workers exposed to
long falls over 6 feet, with workers wearing harnesses and lanyards attached to rebar. What do you do?
a. Call stockholder relations and warn them that some calls may be received and that they should
forward these calls to you.
b. Tell your colleagues that these photographs were published without your review.
c. Review your construction fall protection rules with the Superintendent of Construction.
d. Request to review all photographs of operations before they are used in any future reports.
264 • Active Fall Protection Systems

• Will the method of use force workers to disconnect themselves at
heights because they can’t reach their task?
6. Stability
• Has attachment to the lip of an I-beam flange been prohibited?
A snaphook may slip off with an angled pull and cause system failure.
• Has attaching a lifeline to a projection been prohibited? The lifeline can
detach by slipping off the end.
7. Independence
• Are the anchor points independent? The independence of each
anchor point from the main work-positioning anchor support is an
important principle. Where tripods or the building or structure itself are
concerned, the question to address is, what kind of failure would likely
produce an injury? Anchor-point design should address all predictable
scenarios.
• Is the fall protection system engineered? An engineered system may
permit the lifelines for several workers to be combined, as long as they
are separate from the main work-positioning support.
8. Protection while moving
• If horizontal lifelines are used to allow protected movement, have they
been engineered for this purpose? A horizontal line may be intended as a
hand line or perimeter cable. Termination of lines or butting them with
mechanical clips can be dangerous under dynamic conditions.
• Do the horizontal lines limit sag under the dynamic conditions of a
fall, to permit the worker to avoid colliding with an obstruction or the
ground? Careful analysis of the potential lifeline sag is required to ensure
adequate clearance distance in designed systems.
9. Labeling
• Can the anchor point be marked for future recognition and limited,
specific use? Can workers claim to recognize a 5,000-lb. anchor point, let
alone other criteria, to avoid a predictable system failure in the long run?
Of course not. Many managers simply shrug their shoulders. Putting a
harness and lanyard in the hands of the worker while administering an
admonition to tie off has long been the alibi for fall protection planning
with these managers.
The drawings in Figure 7.2 illustrate six poor choices for anchorage points, based
upon application of the criteria discussed above. The examples in Figure 7.3, on
the other hand, illustrate six good anchorage choices. For a detailed discussion of
testing, labeling, and recertification criteria, see Table 7.2. Two types of permanent
anchorages are illustrated in Figures 7.4 and 7.5.

Preface to the Fourth Edition
The fall-protection revolution has begun! Maybe it was the harness rule in the
United States on January 1, 1998, when harnesses became a requirement and body
belts became illegal for fall arrest. It took only about a year for almost complete
compliance—not only in construction but also in general industry and other
industries. The word got around fast that suspension in a belt was dangerous.
So why is the number and rate of fatal falls still steadily going up? I think there are
two reasons: First, the proper structural anchorage point has not caught on widely
yet (beyond the standard issue of a harness and Y-lanyard). Second, the users of
fall-protection systems do not understand that these systems must be engineered
into the workplace and also maintained with strong, effective programs that
resemble FAA requirements for maintenance of commercial aircraft components.
The program administrator recommended in ANSI Z359.2 can help establish a
stronger role for the Qualified Person and more discipline for the Competent
Person. Advisory standards must begin to focus on incorporation of elements into
the building codes to provide designers with a set of requirements so new buildings
are not immediately in violation of OSHA requirements when the certificate of
occupancy or equivalent is provided.
The Competent Person can help prevent or repair damage that is caused by others
inadvertently and deal with innocent misuse. And as more sophisticated equipment
gets more widely used, there is the tendency to forego critical observations of
how the equipment is actually being used. Supervisors who fail to frequently
monitor work practices, inspect equipment, and check site conditions do so at the
risk of exposing workers to swing falls, cable cutting hazards, rope degradation
under acid conditions, edge hazards, corrosion of cable terminations, SRL pawl
sticking, ground or surface impacts, Y-lanyard deployment hazards, and snaphook
attachment hazards, just to name a few.
This book provides multiple solutions to eliminate fall hazards in more than one
trade or situation and tools to improve fall-hazard observations and documentation.
Recommendations herein for personal training for the exposed worker are vitally
important to reduce exposure to falls, but so too are the many recommendations
for designing out fall hazards and providing engineered anchorages for those who
must maintain buildings long after they are built.
As we march down the road of progress with improved equipment and systems and
standards, let us not forget the importance of the skill of recognizing fall hazards.
Certain exposures, even for a few milliseconds of duration, such as during transitions,
xii • Preface to the Fourth Edition

are potentially lethal and must be addressed by proper training. Even the best
harness with slack webbing adjustment controls and convenient buckle tightening
cannot make up for a poor application or excess fall exposure or nonattachment.
J. Nigel Ellis, Ph.D., PE, CSP, CPE
Introduction to Fall Protection • xiii

Are There Fall Hazards in Every Industry?
Nearly every industry, at some time, engages in work at elevation. The job could
range from the simple use of a 10-foot stepladder to change a light bulb to operating
a powered platform 185 feet up inside a boiler or climbing 200 feet up a flare-stack
ladder. A short, but unique, six-month Bureau of Labor Statistics study (1984)
of approximately 77 elevated-fall injuries showed a variety of industries were
involved. Although injuries in the construction industry were predominant in this
survey (41%), nearly one-fourth of the victims were employed by manufacturers.
Forty-four percent of the injured workers were craft workers, including carpenters
(10%) and mechanics/repairers (6%). A large portion, 24 percent, were working
as laborers, while 12 percent were employed as operators. Other victims included
clerical and sales workers, managers, and transport equipment operators. The
author has found that annually, over the past three decades, the relative numbers
change very little, and surveys may be unique such as this one.
Certain industries, of course, require substantial elevated work. For instance,
frequent elevated tasks associated with transmission and distribution operations in
the utility industry are significantly different from operations within a microchip
processing plant. For those industries, with frequent activity at elevation, the
probability of a fall is consequently higher. In some industries, such as trucking,
the access problems to tank trucks, flatbeds, and soft sides, have hardly begun to
be observed.
There are two types of elevated fall exposure:
1. During Work. Elevated work can be an integral part of a job or trade.
Scalers, for example, whose job it is to remove built-up residue from tanks,
digesters, or vessels, are often exposed to fall hazards, slipping, and chemicals
on an ongoing basis. Other examples, often associated with construction or
maintenance, include roofing, painting, sandblasting, pipe welding, masonry,
or bricklaying, and utility service work. Steel connectors also commonly
work at great elevation.
2. During Access or Exit. In other cases, exposure to a fall hazard occurs
simply while the worker is accessing an elevated workstation. Repair of a
valve, located on the upper tier of a chemical processing pipe rack, may
require that the worker use a fixed ladder 25 to 100 yards away, then walk
the pipe to the valve. Some trades, such as scaffold builders, provide a local
means of access. However, fall protection for these workers, during erection
and dismantling, should not be ignored. Temporary systems can be brought
to the site and removed by the contract scaffold company. Alternatively,
fall protection for access can be provided by the principal/owner and used
throughout the job by other employees.
Access to work areas can provide the greatest hazards, depending upon the
access method selected. Use of a rental van roof to paint signs on an automobile
dealership window is novel but raises questions. Use of a six-foot stepladder, next
to or within a few feet of a guardrail, raises the danger stakes. Running computer
8 • Introduction

lines for process control away from the reach of heavy-duty forklifts puts battery
replacement service 10 feet overhead next to a column. Planning and coordination
is a must for access for repeat visits and especially for single visits. Wiring for the
internet and telecommunications has made utility access a significant hazard above
almost every corridor when old wires are not replaced and new wires follow no
plan for their location.
Often, contractors are brought in to perform elevated work. It could be a
maintenance contract that requires the contractor to climb unprotected towers
and stacks to change aviation warning lights after a letter from the FAA is received
or a complete repair project involving a number of crews. It is still not unusual
to hear a company executive respond, “Oh, we don’t send our people up there—
we contract that out!” This means elevated tasks at a particular worksite can be
accomplished, provided the contractor’s employees are well trained, well equipped,
and guided by solid requirements in the bid document and contractor rulebook
to provide fall protection followed by the necessary site-specific training. This is
especially important to the owner because of third-party legal relationships, which
are not easily appreciated. Therefore, a workable system for establishing and
checking procedures and then observing for compliance is critical and may involve
a local safety consultant to review work if no qualified maintenance person or
safety professional is available.
Falls, caused by slipping or tripping, can lead to more serious elevated falls and
must be addressed (see Chapter 4).
Public fall exposure at elevation is presented primarily by stairs and a myriad of
railing designs, followed by ladders, roofs, and walking close to construction sites.
Tree stands pose a major fall threat to 30 million hunters, which is of particular
interest to employers, who expect their hunter- workers to show up on Mondays
during the hunting season.
Fall Protection from a Historical Perspective
“When one falls, it is not one’s foot that is to blame.”—Chinese proverb
For thousands of years, people have used ropes and various knots to help
move or secure objects against the forces of gravity. Bend knots were used to
gain a reliable hold, and hitch knots were used in moving a load by sliding along
another rope and, if necessary, gripping to lock the load in place. The practice of
people climbing ladders and/or being suspended on ropes and using these same
knots for positioning is primarily an outgrowth of the rigging trades. Some earlier
users would have been found on sailing ships, in church steeple construction and
maintenance, in mines, and in tree-trimming trades.
Ropes and some type of body belt, for restraint or work-positioning support,
were particularly useful during stormy seas and above the decks of ships. A similar
development of harness, rope, and knot usage originated more recently from cliff
and cave rescue, as well as from mountaineering techniques. In the middle 1800s,
Introduction to Fall Protection • 9

The injury is worse when the body part is held rigid in response to reflex or
the fear from actually falling. Human beings are born with a fear of falling. Like
the fear of loud noises, the fear of falling is easily observed in newborns by their
intense grip capability.
Unlike other types of incidents, falls rarely involve near-misses from which
people can be warned or learn about the consequences. However, it is also a well
known fact that falls are underreported. In many cases, the person sustaining a fall is
not injured badly enough to take the time to even report that a fall has occurred. If
they are not seriously injured most people are embarrassed to have fallen. They look
around to see if anyone has seen them fall and then get up as quickly as possible and
scurry off. The National Safety Council publishes Injury Facts every year, reporting
deaths and injuries from falls. These numbers are likely significantly under-reported
too, as many falls occur but are either incorrectly reported or inaccurately reported.
For example, a fall in a restaurant kitchen may result in a worker reaching for support
but inadvertently being burned in a fryer or by a pot of coffee. This scenario would
more than likely result in a report of injury involving a burn, not a fall.
Falls are classified into four general categories: slips, trips, stumbles, and falls
from elevation. Slips, stumbles, and trips, occur on the same level, but can occur
on stairs and on surfaces with elevation changes. Elevated falls occur from one
level to another.
The frequency of slips, stumbles, and trips tends to be very high; however,
when there are injuries, they typically consist of sprains, strains, and ankle injuries.
Conversely, an elevated fall that may only occur every five years, at a particular site,
usually results in serious or fatal injury. If falls on the same level can produce severe
injury, certainly each foot above ground level, increases that likelihood. Table 1.2
provides a brief summary.
Slips and Trips: Causation
A fall occurs to a standing person when the body’s center of gravity is typically
beyond the feet. Since we generally commit the second foot, when the other is still
stepping an obstruction or slip puts us off-balance.
Table 1.2. Loss of Balance Can Lead to Falls
Loss of Balance Results In
Fall.........Elevated fall: fall from one level to another
Trip…… Fall at same level: fall down
Slip……. Fall at same level: fall down
Stair falls may include slips and trips, leading to elevated falls.
Slips and trips may lead to elevated falls, when close to exposed or leading edges.
Slips/Trips: high frequency—low to medium severity, except head injuries—high severity
Elevated Falls: low frequency—high severity
Introduction to Fall Protection • 13

The proper understanding of fall protection results in a commitment to
elimination of fall hazards, and this begins by recognizing fall hazards without
considering the risk. Let the insurance industry worry about the risk. By taking any
route, other than elimination of the hazard altogether, we keep the hazard alive.
Eliminating Fall Hazards
Eliminating fall hazards means finding a way to avoid the necessity of exposure to
heights. This is the number one goal of fall protection. If a hazard is eliminated,
then workers are not put at risk. For example, building a roof truss framework,
fully or partially at ground level, and lifting it into place, is better than assembling
it in the air while standing on the framing.
It’s true that all hazards cannot be eliminated from every particular situation.
However, by addressing the known hazards, we can predict how most of them
can be eliminated or reasonably controlled before workers are exposed to them.
A simple checklist is often all that’s needed because it forces visualization of how
the work is supposed to be done when completed correctly.
Also, simple products that effectively eliminate many fall hazards are available
on the market today. Some examples follow:
• A telescoping duster to remove cobwebs in the office or home. Basically
a dust mop on an extendable pole: this product allows a person to clean
ceilings, skylights, and stairwells without the use of a ladder.
• A fruit harvester. This product consists of a specially designed fruit-picking
basket that clamps onto any long pole. It eliminates fall hazards for workers
harvesting fruit from trees.
• Gutter cleaning device. This product consists of a sprayer that attaches to
a garden hose. An attached, extendable pole lifts the device to gutter level.
When the device is activated, high-pressure water blasts and lifts leaves and
debris from gutters, while the worker remains on the ground.
• Tank truck loading and unloading devices. Tank trucks that can be
loaded and unloaded by workers standing at ground level and eliminate fall
exposures for workers who would otherwise climb to the top of the tank
truck or trailer (Figure 1.13). Work from the ground, by design, requires
proper engineering and order by buyer of this model, for example vapor
recovery systems.
Are Fall Hazards Obvious?
Isn’t it obvious to any person (who may someday sit on a jury) that height hazards
are a known, severe-injury producer, if not a reasonably certain-fatality producer?
Then why don’t employers address this hazard exposure, which can be reasonably
eliminated or controlled? Why is such a severe and foreseeable hazard too often

Foreword
Someone joked, “It’s not the fall that hurts, it’s the sudden stop when you hit the
ground.” Falls have been a core element of clowns’ acts. While these may create
laughs, the problem of falls is serious and a major source of injuries and fatalities.
Slips, trips, and falls have been a safety issue and a large source of insurance and
legal claims for a long, long time.
Early safety literature focused on the equipment and facilities involved in falls, such
as stairs, railings, scaffolds, and so on, but there was little discussion of falls, their
causes and principles, and methods for preventing them and minimizing resulting
injuries.
Some data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics for 2008 reveal that falls remain as
one of the most significant causes of worker deaths. Of 5,071 deaths identified,
13 percent involved falls. Eleven percent involved falls to a lower level. Of the
680 fatal falls, 18 percent were from a roof, 17 percent from a ladder, 12 percent
from a moving vehicle and 10 percent from a scaffold or staging. Among the ten
occupations with the highest job fatality rate were structural iron and steel workers,
roofers, and electrical power-line installers and repairers. According to the Center
for Disease Control statistics, unintentional falls are the leading causes of nonfatal
injuries treated in hospital emergency departments in the United States for all ages
except fifteen- to twenty-four-year-olds, for which it is second. Falls are still a
major safety issue both on the job and outside of work.
This publication is essential for safety professionals. The primary role of safety
professionals, safety engineers, and others practicing in the safety field is prevention.
It is important to educate workers about the hazards found in their occupation and
work. It is important to identify and manage safety programs that help employers
establish a safety culture in their organization. However, preventing injury and
illness is most important. Hazard recognition, evaluation, and control are key.
For engineers, a primary responsibility is protecting the health, safety, and welfare
of the public. They have a responsibility to recognize the hazards involved in the
equipment, facilities, operations, vehicles, and processes they design. They have
the ability to prevent injury by incorporating safety through design. Too often, the
safety professional must take on hazard recognition and prevention of injury after
the design is established. That is why safety professionals need to know almost as
much about a design involving fall hazards as the engineer who created the design
and to ensure protection as the design is implemented.
The author, Dr. Nigel Ellis, has developed this very important publication and now
updated it in the fourth edition. It provides detailed information for preventing
falls. Its major emphasis is on occupational settings involving elevated work.
x • Foreword

Falls are currently the primary cause of death on construction sites and in heavy
industry. Fall protection is a safety system intended to address the hazard of falling.
The forces that accumulate during a fall are astronomical, and upon impact, are
highly injurious, unless a way is found to avert the fall or to sufficiently slow the
body to a safe stop. That is the purpose of this book.
Falling hazards are not always obvious. As an expert witness in front of a jury
in the mid-1990s, I remember being asked to explain why forces on a vertical
rope lifeline are very different from forces impacting a rope strung between two
anchors, known as a horizontal lifeline. It turned out that a rope held between two
anchors, when impacted laterally, could produce forces 16 times greater than those
produced on a vertical lifeline. This was the reason the employer should not have
used ¼-inch-diameter wire rope, which snapped. It was demonstrated that a short
rope held at each end and pulled by two stout anchors (volunteers) could easily be
displaced when pulled laterally with a small finger, thereby dragging the resisting
volunteers with the pulling person in the middle. This shows that the force is
multiplied, but that is not obvious without proper training.
Fall protection, as a safety system, must be planned; it cannot be done on the
spur of the moment. Planning simplifies the training and the work. People who
cling to the popular misconception that all safety is an expense are amazed to find
that productivity has repeatedly been shown to increase by as much as 35 percent
when safety is made a priority.
This fourth edition of the book is for those striving for effective fall protection
and who regularly meet with discussion, but no decision or just silence, when
fall hazards are brought up. It is written to encourage perseverance in a noble
lifesaving undertaking. Fall-hazard recognition and acceptance are the start of the
fall-solution process.
Recent statistics on falls are worse than those of previous years according to
the Bureau of Labor Statistics (with the exception of 2008 and 2009, years of
economic recession); fall fatalities have been rising by an average of 10 percent
each year. During the same time period, overall work fatalities had been on the
decline. However, since an initial drop in 2002, overall fatalities and fatal falls
trended up again; fatal falls exceeded the previous high of 810 in 2004 and 2006,
while overall work fatalities stayed below 2001 fatalities (BLS 2011) (see Table 1.1).
Falls are the leading causes of nonfatal unintentional injuries that are treated
in hospital emergency rooms (ERs), totaling 21 percent of all treated injuries,

according to data from the All Injury Program, a cooperative program involving
the National Center for Injury Prevention and Control,Centers for Disease Control
(CDC), and the Consumer Product Safety Commission. Nearly eight million people
were treated in an ER for fall-related injuries in 2005. Falls were the leading cause of
nonfatal injuries for all age groups except 15–24 year olds, for which struck, by or
against an object or person, was the leading cause (Injury Facts). Further discussion
on the leading causes of occupational injuries, is in the sidebar on page 3.
Emergency Room Data Provide Important
Information about Leading Causes of Injury
Unintentional falls are the leading cause of injury and the
second most common cause of occupational injury deaths
in the United States; they place a great burden on emergency
rooms. In this study, the objective was to describe the inci-
dence and characteristics of emergency room (ER) visits
associated with unintentional falls in the United States.
Methods: The authors performed a secondary analysis on
data from the National Center for Health Statistics National
Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey for 1992–1994.
An ER visit was defined as fall-related if an ICD-9-CM
cause of injury code was reported as E880.0-886.9 or E888.
Results: There were an estimated 7,946,000 fall-related
ER visits per year, corresponding to an annual rate of 3.1
per 100 persons (95% CI = 2.8 to 3.4). Children under 5
years of age, comprised the largest proportion of visits
(14%). Among those visits, coded with respect to place of
occurrence, the rate of visits, associated with falls, occur-
ring at home (1.7/100; 95% CI = 1.6 to 1.9) was signifi-
cantly higher, than that associated with falls, occurring in all
other locations combined (1.1/100; 95% CI = 1.0 to 1.2).
The mean injury-severity score increased significantly with
the age of the patient. Fall-related ER visits resulted in an
estimated 860,000 hospitalizations, 62 percent of which
involved individuals aged 65 years and older. An estimated
$2.45 billion per year was paid for fall-related ER visits. Gov-
ernment sources paid all or part of 41 percent of visits.
Conclusions: This study reports nationally representa-
tive data describing the incidence and characteristics of fall-
related ER visits. These data expand what is known about
the epidemiology of falls and help to define the burden that
fall injuries place on ERs in the United States. The results of
this study could serve as a benchmark to evaluate the effec-
tiveness of future fall prevention efforts.
Courtesy the Academy of Emergency Medicine. For updates and further
information, refer to www.Medscape.com.

Standards Around the World: Status Relative to the United States
The United States still trails behind many foreign countries relative to the requirements
of its standards and the degree of fall protection offered to many workers.
The Canadian Ministry of Labour administers Canada’s national fall protection

(CSA) guidelines continue to advance on the issue of fall arrest equipment
component standards.

considerably more advanced in this area of safety standards. For example, in 1978,
France banned the use of a body belt to meet its national fall arrest requirements.
A year later, Britain followed suit by limiting the use of body belts to where free

Corporate Counsel of Knowledgeable Principals
Attorneys should carefully review a company’s bid documents. Wording should
be added to require compliance with the company’s safety rules, especially fall
protection rules, so that standards can be maintained by contractors. Gone are
the days, in most jurisdictions, when one could rely solely upon the exculpatory
contract wording, “Contractor must meet local, city, state, and OSHA safety
rules,” not because it is untrue but because it is incomplete. The knowledgeable
owner must require contractors to fulfill these obligations to help avoid third-
party tort claims (Philo 1979). Corporate counsel should ask the question, “Who is
responsible for the integrity of any anchorage point on the property?”
The knowledgeable owner also must know that many contractors will not follow
general safety rules—they are presently exempt from responsibility under Workers’
Compensation laws in most jurisdictions, and the insurance carrier will be made
whole if the third-party suit succeeds. It is critical that an owner aim to solve the
most predictable cause of loss: that incurred from elevated falls. A company’s loss
is guaranteed unless preventive measures are taken at the contract stage. Even
an indemnity clause signed by the contractor must, at some stage, be negotiated.
Elevated-work fall hazards no longer should be viewed as ordinary risk.
Corporate counsel should work closely and proactively with the corporate
safety director in training and education regarding legal liability and should actively
participate in the company’s preventive safety engineering program.2 The following
are some initiatives a firm can practice:
• Educate supervisors and safety personnel in the standards of care required
for a project.
• Teach doctrines of liability and the Restatement of Torts as they apply in
specific jurisdictions.
• Explain the legal tests for liability of parties, including all invitees.
• Discuss recent cases involving the company to point out lessons learned.
• Explain project contract safety requirements.
Consulting Engineers—Civil, Structural, Design, Project, Industrial
Owners, engineers, and architects for buildings, bridges, dams, and other civil or
industrial projects must demonstrate that construction at each stage can be done
with reasonable safe access and reasonable fall protection. Anchorage-strength
design should minimally equal twice the maximum force of the fall system that will
be attached to the anchorage. Designing for fall protection should follow shock and
vibration engineering’s 2:1 minimum factor for engineered systems, as opposed to
the 5:1 or higher wear-and-tear factor frequently used in industry. (Note: Be sure to
evaluate for corrosion and misuse, such as that which occurs at lifting points.) Under
most circumstances, a 5,000-lb. anchor strength requirement is easily obtainable.
However, where specific situations limit anchor selection or design, the strength

Equipment and Prefab Manufacturers
Those companies who make material-handling or access equipment are at risk if
they have not considered fall hazards and escape modes from buckets, platforms,
oil rigs, tanks, racks, crane cabs, and scaffolds during both erection and subsequent
maintenance procedures.
Warnings that clearly depict falling hazards are the first line of awareness for
workers or inspectors exposed to fall hazards during equipment operation or
maintenance. Going beyond warnings to propose the method of fall protection is
an important goal for equipment manufacturers.
A practical method of fall protection should be proposed by rig, equipment, and
scaffold manufacturers or guidance provided by scaffold associations that mirrors
the anticipated or foreseeable (what’s known or likely) work method. Anchorage
points (or instructions for them) should be provided to suit this anticipated need.
Examples of equipment and types of prefab manufacturers who need to think
out how their installers, equipment users, or maintainers should be protected from
falls are shown in Table 3.1.
Scaffold manufacturers should detail fall protection methods during erection
in their instructions. Scissors-lift manufacturers, recognizing that workers may use
the midrailings as a ladder rung to reach up to and in between an obstruction, may
decide that a grating or mesh could be installed to limit this fall-exposure tendency.
However, it also makes sense for manufacturers to specify personal fall protection
systems for overreaching or leaning over guardrails.
Lack of means of escape from these high workstations means that, in an
emergency, the workers could be trapped. For example, a slow-to-respond bucket
truck could be a problem if a swarm of bees attacks an elevated operator who is
clearing vegetation, causing the worker to jump out. Manufacturers must address
this type of problem once they become aware of even a single occurrence or
believe the scenario may occur. Oil-drilling and service rig manufacturers need to
address the problems of derrickmen in emergency situations by detailing the types
of work-positioning fall arrest and controlled-descent systems that are practical
and then making provisions for their installation. One system cannot provide
adequate work positioning, fall protection, and climbing protection.
In some industries vibration can contribute to fall hazards, such as for yarders
in the logging industry, and those operating pile drivers. Selecting fall protection
equipment that does not contribute or even amplify vibration is imperative to
lessening fatigue resulting from long-term vibration exposure. Tank manufacturers
need to address maintenance-work methods with practical access and fall protection.
Tank and vessel manufacturers must be sure to design manways greater than
eighteen inches in diameter to avoid trapping both workers and rescuers; a twenty-
four-inch minimum should be considered. In particular, maintainers of digester
tanks in the pulp industry should have access systems specified in instructions and
should recommend practical fall protection and emergency retrieval systems.

Jumping
Jumping over an obstruction or puddle is tempting, but it should be avoided at
work. Attempting to jump over a unit skylight can terminate with a lethal result.
It is wiser to use good judgment and walk around obstacles. Note: Teenagers who
gain access to the roof of their school or other property as a cool secluded spot
may try to not only sit on but also to trampoline jump on an unprotected dome
skylight. Several are killed in such incidents each year in the United States.
Stairways and Ramps
Just as expectation is a centrally important concept for missteps described in the
previous section, it is even more important when the underfoot walking surface
changes elevation, either because of an abrupt slope change or because of a step,
projecting lip, or drop-off.
Types of Missteps
Misstep is not another word for a mistake made in ambulation; it is the increasingly
used technical term for “an unintentional departure from the pedestrian gait
appropriate for the walkway surface.” This definition comes from the chapter
“A Guide to Human Factors Terminology” in the Handbook of Human Factors in
Litigation (Thompson 2005). The authors add: “If the misstep results in a loss
of balance and the pedestrian does not recover that balance, a fall may result.”
It also contrasts and compares the term to “slip, trip, and fall.” Examples of
missteps also defined in the Handbook include air step, heel scuff, overstep, understep, and
unstable footing, beyond the traditional slips and trips. Jake Pauls has championed
usage of the general term missteps and the consideration of specific types of
missteps going beyond the traditional—and often too loosely used—terms slip
and trip (Pauls 2007 and Pauls and Harbuck 2008).
The other types of missteps have particular relevance to falls that occur on
stairways and ramps or, more generally, walking surfaces where there is a change in
elevation by virtue of a step or change in slope. Pedestrians must have a realistic
expectation of the presence and nature of such elevation changes, especially when
they encounter a drop in the walking surface that is not visually obvious. Such
drops, even with elevation changes of as little as an inch, encourage a particularly
jarring form of unexpected footfall known as an air step. Air steps at drops of less
than about seven inches are particularly jarring, as one’s body cannot react to the
drop fast enough, and the resulting injuries (to ankles, knees, hips, and backs) can
occur even if the person does not lose balance with a resulting full-body fall to the
walking surface (Jones and Watt 1971).
Additionally, the use of bifocals can cause a trip hazard; as one looks down, the
footing surface is not visually clear and may cause a slip, trip, or fall.

evidence_basis.supporting_text:
Falls are currently the primary cause of death on construction sites and in heavy
industry. Fall protection is a safety system intended to address the hazard of falling.
The forces that accumulate during a fall are astronomical, and upon impact, are
highly injurious, unless a way is found to avert the fall or to sufficiently slow the
body to a safe stop. That is the purpose of this book.
Falling hazards are not always obvious. As an expert witness in front of a jury
in the mid-1990s, I remember being asked to explain why forces on a vertical
rope lifeline are very different from forces impacting a rope strung between two
anchors, known as a horizontal lifeline. It turned out that a rope held between two
anchors, when impacted laterally, could produce forces 16 times greater than those
produced on a vertical lifeline. This was the reason the employer should not have
used ¼-inch-diameter wire rope, which snapped. It was demonstrated that a short
rope held at each end and pulled by two stout anchors (volunteers) could easily be
displaced when pulled laterally with a small finger, thereby dragging the resisting
volunteers with the pulling person in the middle. This shows that the force is
multiplied, but that is not obvious without proper training.
Fall protection, as a safety system, must be planned; it cannot be done on the
spur of the moment. Planning simplifies the training and the work. People who
cling to the popular misconception that all safety is an expense are amazed to find
that productivity has repeatedly been shown to increase by as much as 35 percent
when safety is made a priority.
This fourth edition of the book is for those striving for effective fall protection
and who regularly meet with discussion, but no decision or just silence, when
fall hazards are brought up. It is written to encourage perseverance in a noble
lifesaving undertaking. Fall-hazard recognition and acceptance are the start of the
fall-solution process.
Recent statistics on falls are worse than those of previous years according to
the Bureau of Labor Statistics (with the exception of 2008 and 2009, years of
economic recession); fall fatalities have been rising by an average of 10 percent
each year. During the same time period, overall work fatalities had been on the
decline. However, since an initial drop in 2002, overall fatalities and fatal falls
trended up again; fatal falls exceeded the previous high of 810 in 2004 and 2006,
while overall work fatalities stayed below 2001 fatalities (BLS 2011) (see Table 1.1).
Falls are the leading causes of nonfatal unintentional injuries that are treated
in hospital emergency rooms (ERs), totaling 21 percent of all treated injuries,

2 • Introduction

With revised Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) fall
protection standards that took effect in 1995, every business was readying for an
OSHA crackdown. It never came. Congress, in 1994, prevented the enforcement
of OSHA roofing standards. The roofing industry, particularly in residential
construction, was the main focus of the revised standards. Roofing contractors
stopped buying fall protection, even at give-away prices; manufacturers put roof
brackets on the junk pile as scrap. The cost of this deferment is being realized
in the continuing toll of fatalities and permanent disabling injuries (multiply
fatalities by 300). Roofs, scaffolds, and ladders make up the majority of fatal fall
hazards.
The cost of fall protection is measured not just in lives and dollars but also in
the currency of engineering, equipment, training, and enforcement. It is a tragedy
that personal injury attorneys are frequently searching for solutions to prevent fall
incidents to a greater extent than some safety departments. Understandably, there
are many hazards that industry must recognize and analyze—in contrast to the
attorneys, who need only focus on the one hazard that led to a specific incident.
Elimination of fall hazards is the only long-term solution for organizations currently
planning a new project. That means engineering solutions must be determined at
the design and planning stages.
Companies unfamiliar with the new standards continue to allow their workers
to accept the risk of falling from structures. General contractors delegate work to
their subcontractors—often believing they have delegated the responsibility for
safety. Industry often relies on general, undocumented training merely reading
regulations to employees or signing an attendance sheet for a nonexistent safety
meeting; little relevant testing or observation or retraining are done to ensure a
competent workforce on-site. Many government contracts for construction and
repair (e.g., bridges) tend to place the entire safety responsibility on the general
contractor (or its equivalent by contract). Safety measures are then practically
unenforced, as subcontractors go about their business with hustle, cutting costs,
and time, wherever they can, to meet deadlines that may carry a financial penalty.
Owners easily overlook how proper architectural design and engineering, or
construction sequence, doing as much on the ground as possible, can eliminate
many serious fall hazards. What is missing is the field of engineering planning,
which some larger corporations implemented many years ago.
There are notable exceptions to outdated practices, such as the enlightened
approaches within empowered workforces, in firms that have made a safety
breakthrough and can carve out business niches based upon safety, particularly
fall-hazard solutions. Professionalism and pride in teamwork can then be restored.
Juries fundamentally know that gravity always works on the earth, despite TV
and movie-screen stunts and cartoons to the contrary. However, jurors are not sure
whether injured workers knew they would be severely injured or killed if they fell.
For some victims, the fall is a death sentence. And only a fall survivor knows the
agony and despair of experiencing lifelong pain or disability.
4 • Introduction

lines for process control away from the reach of heavy-duty forklifts puts battery
replacement service 10 feet overhead next to a column. Planning and coordination
is a must for access for repeat visits and especially for single visits. Wiring for the
internet and telecommunications has made utility access a significant hazard above
almost every corridor when old wires are not replaced and new wires follow no
plan for their location.
Often, contractors are brought in to perform elevated work. It could be a
maintenance contract that requires the contractor to climb unprotected towers
and stacks to change aviation warning lights after a letter from the FAA is received
or a complete repair project involving a number of crews. It is still not unusual
to hear a company executive respond, “Oh, we don’t send our people up there—
we contract that out!” This means elevated tasks at a particular worksite can be
accomplished, provided the contractor’s employees are well trained, well equipped,
and guided by solid requirements in the bid document and contractor rulebook
to provide fall protection followed by the necessary site-specific training. This is
especially important to the owner because of third-party legal relationships, which
are not easily appreciated. Therefore, a workable system for establishing and
checking procedures and then observing for compliance is critical and may involve
a local safety consultant to review work if no qualified maintenance person or
safety professional is available.
Falls, caused by slipping or tripping, can lead to more serious elevated falls and
must be addressed (see Chapter 4).
Public fall exposure at elevation is presented primarily by stairs and a myriad of
railing designs, followed by ladders, roofs, and walking close to construction sites.
Tree stands pose a major fall threat to 30 million hunters, which is of particular
interest to employers, who expect their hunter- workers to show up on Mondays
during the hunting season.
Fall Protection from a Historical Perspective
“When one falls, it is not one’s foot that is to blame.”—Chinese proverb
For thousands of years, people have used ropes and various knots to help
move or secure objects against the forces of gravity. Bend knots were used to
gain a reliable hold, and hitch knots were used in moving a load by sliding along
another rope and, if necessary, gripping to lock the load in place. The practice of
people climbing ladders and/or being suspended on ropes and using these same
knots for positioning is primarily an outgrowth of the rigging trades. Some earlier
users would have been found on sailing ships, in church steeple construction and
maintenance, in mines, and in tree-trimming trades.
Ropes and some type of body belt, for restraint or work-positioning support,
were particularly useful during stormy seas and above the decks of ships. A similar
development of harness, rope, and knot usage originated more recently from cliff
and cave rescue, as well as from mountaineering techniques. In the middle 1800s,
Introduction to Fall Protection • 9

The proper understanding of fall protection results in a commitment to
elimination of fall hazards, and this begins by recognizing fall hazards without
considering the risk. Let the insurance industry worry about the risk. By taking any
route, other than elimination of the hazard altogether, we keep the hazard alive.
Eliminating Fall Hazards
Eliminating fall hazards means finding a way to avoid the necessity of exposure to
heights. This is the number one goal of fall protection. If a hazard is eliminated,
then workers are not put at risk. For example, building a roof truss framework,
fully or partially at ground level, and lifting it into place, is better than assembling
it in the air while standing on the framing.
It’s true that all hazards cannot be eliminated from every particular situation.
However, by addressing the known hazards, we can predict how most of them
can be eliminated or reasonably controlled before workers are exposed to them.
A simple checklist is often all that’s needed because it forces visualization of how
the work is supposed to be done when completed correctly.
Also, simple products that effectively eliminate many fall hazards are available
on the market today. Some examples follow:
• A telescoping duster to remove cobwebs in the office or home. Basically
a dust mop on an extendable pole: this product allows a person to clean
ceilings, skylights, and stairwells without the use of a ladder.
• A fruit harvester. This product consists of a specially designed fruit-picking
basket that clamps onto any long pole. It eliminates fall hazards for workers
harvesting fruit from trees.
• Gutter cleaning device. This product consists of a sprayer that attaches to
a garden hose. An attached, extendable pole lifts the device to gutter level.
When the device is activated, high-pressure water blasts and lifts leaves and
debris from gutters, while the worker remains on the ground.
• Tank truck loading and unloading devices. Tank trucks that can be
loaded and unloaded by workers standing at ground level and eliminate fall
exposures for workers who would otherwise climb to the top of the tank
truck or trailer (Figure 1.13). Work from the ground, by design, requires
proper engineering and order by buyer of this model, for example vapor
recovery systems.
Are Fall Hazards Obvious?
Isn’t it obvious to any person (who may someday sit on a jury) that height hazards
are a known, severe-injury producer, if not a reasonably certain-fatality producer?
Then why don’t employers address this hazard exposure, which can be reasonably
eliminated or controlled? Why is such a severe and foreseeable hazard too often

Tools for Safety
Walls, railings, floors, perimeter cables, scaffolds, and aerial platforms are the first
choice for fall prevention. These structures act as guards.
In general, however, there are two types of equipment used at heights—work-
positioning equipment and fall arrest equipment. Understanding the difference can
help prevent catastrophic injuries.
If the worker’s weight is actively and steadily applied to the equipment to help
the worker do the job hands-free, that is work-positioning equipment. For example,
a lineman typically leans on a belt and strap system. There is no energy-absorbing
factor. There is a potentially heavy-wear factor.
Fall arrest equipment, however, should be passive. The only force to be seen,
other than the weight of the equipment itself, is dynamic force during an accidental
fall arrest. For this, energy-absorbing features are vital to help avoid serious injury.
Introduction to Fall Protection • 33

David MacCollum’s “Safe Design Hierarchy to Physically Control Hazards,”
includes the consideration of safety factors, and redundancy, in addition to hazard
elimination and guarding. Safety factors, argues MacCollum, should be increased, so
that structural strengths are raised above the foreseeable misuse and wear limits or
that non-slip surfaces provide much more than the required amount of traction to
reduce failures. Redundancy, using a series of safeguards, each of which must fail
before the system fails, further increases the safety of the overall system. Figure 1.17
shows the MacCollum Hazard Matrix. This matrix can be used to identify and
address hazards at the time of design or project planning. In MacCollum’s book,
Construction Safety Engineering Principles, he explains that as construction projects
become more complex and sophisticated, safety must be addressed with the
same attention to technical detail, as is applied to the engineering of the projects
themselves. The project critical path should be highlighted at those points where
hazards have been identified in order to recognize potential problem areas. Listing
hazards in this fashion forces the planner to consider itemized alternatives, leading to
the application of a systems safety approach—the same approach that has become
the backbone of aerospace and nuclear energy design. MacCollum recommends
that manufacturers of steel formwork for columns and similar elevated work places
include safety-line anchor attachments and permanent ladder systems for access.
Architects should design permanent attachment opportunities into elevated
locations for both builders and maintenance workers. Designs calling for installation of
permanent guardrails around rooftops eliminates the possibility of falls during many
construction and maintenance activities. Christiansen and Manuele view this as a part
of the entire safety-through-design process that integrates safety in product design and
manufacturing processes with facility design, thereby fostering a “safety first” approach
throughout. By moving safety “upstream” in the design process, safety is more easily
implemented both in manufacturing and in maintenance (see Figure 1.18).

Confined Space Entry and Control with personal fall protection.
Retrieval Operations
Method of Vertical Access Back-up fall protection is needed.
(either fixed or temporary)
Vertical Retrieval Method • Manual mechanical means suitable for up to 50 feet.
• Power mechanical means (with manual back-up) may be more suitable over
50 feet.
• Minimum of 4:1 mechanical advantage; 6:1 or 8:1 preferable to allow one stand-by
person to retrieve a victim.
Retrieval Time Should be under 4 minutes to help avoid permanent brain damage (cardiac and
respiratory arrest victims) unless alternate life support means are established.
User with Respiratory A spreader bar and yoke configuration attached to shoulder D-rings avoids
Equipment interference and enables vertical lifts through smaller openings.
Full Body Harness Can provide proper support during suspension and can position the body vertically
for retrieval through the opening. Can be combined into work suits to help keep the
harness clean.
Narrow Openings If a small opening diameter requires the arms to be overhead, wristlets can be used
to hold up the arms, but a harness should always be used to lift the body weight,
to avoid the possibility of arm dislocation. Some openings are so small that they
should not be entered even by a small worker, in case he or she needs to be rescued.
OSHA is recommending a 24-inch opening as a minimum size for entry.
Entry and Retrieval
These four points form the foundation for any discussion and implementation of
entry and retrieval in confined spaces:
• The ANSI Z117.1 standard stresses training.
• The OSHA 1910.146, published in 1993, requires employers to designate
whether the confined space is permit-required or nonpermit-required.
• Re-designation is required annually.
• Harnesses and mechanical winches are required for depths over 5 feet.
Entering confined spaces such as vessels, storage tanks, ship compartments, silos,
pits, tunnels, vaults, and pipelines often involves exposure to a fall hazard, in addition
to introducing a potential need for emergency retrieval. By design, many confined
spaces have limited openings for entry and egress. And, if potentially toxic conditions
can be present, there is the added danger that rescue workers may be overcome and
trapped as well. Venting and performing test procedures are essential prior to entry,
as well as using the proper personal protective equipment, and rescue equipment.
Many safety professionals agree that work-crew extrication is an essential
ingredient of training programs for confined space work. Crew removal from
the confined space is an ideal starting point in a program for rescue teams.

The Program Administrator
The person in charge of the development, implementation, and monitoring of the
fall protection and rescue program is defined as the program administrator. The
responsibilities of the administrator include providing guidance to all individuals
and departments affected by the fall protection program, providing training
programs, participating in accident investigations, and evaluating the effectiveness
of the program.
The program administrator should ideally be a senior member of management
who, in addition to having authority to enforce the rules, regulations, and standards
across the entire site, has the ability to obtain funding for fall protection training
and equipment.
The program administrator’s first step in developing a fall protection and rescue
program is to define the scope of the program. This means defining who the
program applies to, the locations where the policy will be in force, and the date the
policy enters into force. This also includes assigning all duties and responsibilities,
including Qualified Person, Competent Person, and Authorized Person.
The Competent Person
According to OSHA regulations, “competent and qualified persons” are a necessary
requirement for a fall protection program. OSHA 1926.32 defines a Competent
Person as: “a person who is capable of identifying existing and predictable hazards
in the surroundings or identifying working conditions which are hazardous or
dangerous to employees and who has authorization to take prompt corrective
measures to eliminate them.”
The ANSI Fall Protection Code Z359.0-2007 defines the Competent Person
as “an individual designated by the employer to be responsible for the immediate
supervision, implementation, and monitoring of the employer’s managed fall
protection program who, through training and knowledge, is capable of identifying,
evaluating, and addressing existing and potential fall hazards, and who has the
employer’s authority to take prompt corrective action with regard to such hazards.”
The Competent Person acts as the immediate supervisor of the fall protection
program. Responsibilities of this position include conducting fall-hazard surveys,
identifying potential fall hazards, and stopping or limiting work until hazards
are addressed, supervising the selection and use of equipment, verifying that
equipment is compliant and that workers are trained, participating in accident
and near-miss investigations, conducting equipment inspections, and removing
damaged equipment from service (ANSI Z359.0 – 2007).
When work is performed at elevation, OSHA requires that a Competent Person
be at the job site (not at home during off shifts). He or she is responsible for
ensuring that the work at elevation has been properly planned and is properly
implemented. The Competent Person must also periodically monitor the job while
it is being performed to insure that the plan is being followed and that work is
being done safely.

Overall, an audit (examples of numerous types are published) can be used to
assess the effectiveness of the fall protection program. It is an opportunity to see
if previously set objectives have been met and to determine what changes need to
be made.
Fall protection programs often flounder early in their implementation because
too many details are left unaddressed. An audit committee is a good way to point
out weaknesses and focus on removing blockages to progress.
A program audit encompasses organized, periodic testing to ensure that the
objectives of a fall protection program are met. Regular evaluation of the effectiveness
of the managed fall protection program is a critical component in eliminating and
controlling fall hazards. This involves a continuous process of building on program
strengths and correcting deficiencies. The evaluations should examine the program
to determine whether it has accomplished its objectives and whether they have been
achieved according to the written program.
Safety personnel from another plant typically perform these audits. Using
checklists, they ask questions pertaining to training records, work methods,
incident records, content of training, remediation, and work practices, with respect
to established fall protection and the planning for fall protection solutions in
upcoming projects.
Review of audit results should be conducted to point out the successes and also
the shortcomings flagged by the audit. The results should be published to show
workers and management their progress. These results can also be used to set new
goals, as a result of input from all exposed workers and their supervisors. Part of
continuous improvement includes regularly scheduled program reviews and drills,
such as rescue drills.
The program administrator should evaluate program effectiveness periodically—
at least every two years, when Authorized Persons or Competent Persons identify
deficiencies, or when there are incidents involving injuries, property damage, or
near misses.
The documented program evaluation shall identify, for each element: program
strengths, program deficiencies, and recommendations for improvement. A
documented plan of action shall then be developed to identify what changes will
be made, who is responsible for making each change, and when the change will be
completed.
Program evaluations shall be retained on file for at least five years, longer if
mandated by a legislative authority.
Return on Investment
In the author’s experience, a serious or fatal injury occurs at an average of every
five to ten years in companies where workers are regularly exposed to elevated fall
hazards. Although this number may seem low relative to other injuries, the severity
of fall incidents is usually very high and typically produces lifelong consequences.
The cost of instituting a comprehensive fall protection program is negligible in
comparison to the economic benefits an employer receives. Because the severity
of a single fall incident is so high, whatever the existing general insurance and

Labor supplied by union halls pose a unique challenge for companies seeking

When workers understand that the issues go beyond simply keeping a job or a
high pay scale, then roofers, laborers, overhand bricklayers, steel connectors, and
others will look for better access and for safety from the fall hazards that threaten
their livelihood.

Self-contained emergency-escape chutes capable of evacuating 30 to 40 persons
per minute await adoption in the United States for building and industrial use.
Japan and Europe are current users of these systems. The Japanese fire code
includes the use of escape chutes. These can be utilized vertically, or at an angle
if supervised. Vertical chutes have an internal spiral design to slow descent to a
comfortable rate. Escape chutes should provide inherent descent-speed control up
to approximately 10 feet per second and reasonably ensure a continuous descent
to a soft touchdown at the bottom.
Offshore-platform escape provisions for groups of 20 or 30 at a time, for
instance, require suitable automatically controlled systems to give reliable access
to water level. For cold-water emergency use on rigs and platforms, self-contained
capsules, which also serve as navigable escape craft, provide controlled descent.
Personal controlled-descent devices or approved means of abandonment
(U.S. Coast Guard) are required for evacuation from offshore platforms.
Emergency-Escape Training
Training is the key to the successful use of any emergency egress procedure or
device. Comprehensive and frequently repeated training sessions without exposure
to height under 10 feet, for example, help to overcome the panic that may confuse
or even paralyze workers in an emergency situation. Equipment must be reliable,
visible, simple to operate, and thoroughly familiar to the workers whose lives
may depend on it. Some equipment manufacturers have prepared manuals and
consulting services to assist with employee training programs.
Personal Rescue Systems
Competent Rescue teams develop techniques for the recovery of workers who
may be injured or trapped in difficult positions. It is important to remember that
when rescuing an injured or sick worker from a workstation, time is critical. The
first few minutes for a heart attack victim, for example, can be vital.
Many lives can be saved if employers build rescue techniques into their workplace
operations. These rescue techniques would require less skill and training than those
used by highly trained rescue squads.
If safety lines (e.g., ropes and cables) are used for manual hand-over-hand or
block-and-tackle rescue, they should have a minimum breaking strength of 2,650
lbs., according to OSHA. Chafing over sharp edges should be avoided to prevent
weakening the system.
If space permits, a stretcher or basket should be used to support the victim,
but in tanks with small manhole entrances, wristlets in combination with body
harnesses and suitable D-ring locations can be used to hold the worker in a vertical
position during the retrieval process. A safety feature should be incorporated
to prevent falling back into the manhole. Figure 12.8 presents a list of selection
criteria for personal emergency-descent systems.

Measuring instruments have sensitivity represented in hertz (Hz). The force
transducer, which is used to measure maximum arresting force (MAF), can register
from 0.1 Hz to 10,000+ Hz. However, the test rig may interfere with test results
obtained as low as 250 Hz and produce spurious values, unless these undesirable
frequencies are filtered. In Britain, for many years, a 1,000-Hz sensitivity level was
chosen. But the human body is a much better energy absorber than a steel weight,
and the exact reproducibility of a drop is difficult, so the midheight of the wave
documented by the force transducer in a fall test was deemed the appropriate force
level.
Work done by Harry Crawford of the National Engineering Labs in Scotland
for the British Standards Institute has shown that a sensitivity of 100 Hz is a more
than adequate force measurement for personal fall devices.7 Ulysse and Sulowski
(1982) have shown that a steel test weight produces a force 20 percent to 50
percent higher than an anthropomorphic dummy does. And Chen Wang estimated
that steel weights create forces 50 percent to 100 percent higher than the human
body (Wang 1977). OSHA has adopted a 1.4:1 force factor of a steel weight to
the human body. In the United States, a maximum sensitivity level of 100–125 Hz
has been proposed, derived from a report to the ANSI Z359 committee by Jim
Brinkley of the Aerospace Medical Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air
Force Base. This recommendation is based upon ejection studies, cadaver skull
resonance, and related data (Brinkley et. al 1986).
At 100 or 125 Hz, the actual dynamic peak should be recorded when a fall
system’s arrest force is charted. (See the graphs in Figures 6.27 and 6.28 for the
measurement of MAF and force-test demonstrations, respectively). All resonance
due to the test rig and other unrelated peaks can then be eliminated or disregarded.

Entry and Retrieval
These four points form the foundation for any discussion and implementation of
entry and retrieval in confined spaces:
• The ANSI Z117.1 standard stresses training.
• The OSHA 1910.146, published in 1993, requires employers to designate
whether the confined space is permit-required or nonpermit-required.
• Re-designation is required annually.
• Harnesses and mechanical winches are required for depths over 5 feet.
Entering confined spaces such as vessels, storage tanks, ship compartments, silos,
pits, tunnels, vaults, and pipelines often involves exposure to a fall hazard, in addition
to introducing a potential need for emergency retrieval. By design, many confined
spaces have limited openings for entry and egress. And, if potentially toxic conditions
can be present, there is the added danger that rescue workers may be overcome and
trapped as well. Venting and performing test procedures are essential prior to entry,
as well as using the proper personal protective equipment, and rescue equipment.
Many safety professionals agree that work-crew extrication is an essential
ingredient of training programs for confined space work. Crew removal from
the confined space is an ideal starting point in a program for rescue teams.

The Program Administrator
The person in charge of the development, implementation, and monitoring of the
fall protection and rescue program is defined as the program administrator. The
responsibilities of the administrator include providing guidance to all individuals
and departments affected by the fall protection program, providing training
programs, participating in accident investigations, and evaluating the effectiveness
of the program.
The program administrator should ideally be a senior member of management
who, in addition to having authority to enforce the rules, regulations, and standards
across the entire site, has the ability to obtain funding for fall protection training
and equipment.
The program administrator’s first step in developing a fall protection and rescue
program is to define the scope of the program. This means defining who the
program applies to, the locations where the policy will be in force, and the date the
policy enters into force. This also includes assigning all duties and responsibilities,
including Qualified Person, Competent Person, and Authorized Person.
The Competent Person
According to OSHA regulations, “competent and qualified persons” are a necessary
requirement for a fall protection program. OSHA 1926.32 defines a Competent
Person as: “a person who is capable of identifying existing and predictable hazards
in the surroundings or identifying working conditions which are hazardous or
dangerous to employees and who has authorization to take prompt corrective
measures to eliminate them.”
The ANSI Fall Protection Code Z359.0-2007 defines the Competent Person
as “an individual designated by the employer to be responsible for the immediate
supervision, implementation, and monitoring of the employer’s managed fall
protection program who, through training and knowledge, is capable of identifying,
evaluating, and addressing existing and potential fall hazards, and who has the
employer’s authority to take prompt corrective action with regard to such hazards.”
The Competent Person acts as the immediate supervisor of the fall protection
program. Responsibilities of this position include conducting fall-hazard surveys,
identifying potential fall hazards, and stopping or limiting work until hazards
are addressed, supervising the selection and use of equipment, verifying that
equipment is compliant and that workers are trained, participating in accident
and near-miss investigations, conducting equipment inspections, and removing
damaged equipment from service (ANSI Z359.0 – 2007).
When work is performed at elevation, OSHA requires that a Competent Person
be at the job site (not at home during off shifts). He or she is responsible for
ensuring that the work at elevation has been properly planned and is properly
implemented. The Competent Person must also periodically monitor the job while
it is being performed to insure that the plan is being followed and that work is
being done safely.

OSHA fall protection regulations for construction define the roles of fall
protection Competent Persons on construction sites. Competent persons may
perform different supervisory roles:
1. The Competent Person must have the authority to shut down the job if it
is not being done safely and according to the fall protection plan [OSHA
1926.502(k)].
2. The individual responsible for fall protection training must be a Competent
Person [1926.503 (a)(2)].
3. A Competent Person must periodically inspect fall protection equipment
and insure that employees know how to inspect their own equipment.
4. A safety monitor must be a Competent Person to warn others of roof edge
fall hazards within a controlled-access zone.
5. A fall protection plan must be implemented by a Competent Person.
These Competent Persons may be different persons who have different training
and different responsibilities.
The Competent Person must be provided with the proper authority, resources,
and assistance needed to perform his or her responsibilities. The Competent Person
should consult with and obtain information from authorized persons affected by the
facility fall protection program and procedures. This kind of feedback from the
users of the program is necessary for determining the success of the program and
the need for improvements or additions to the program.
It is not expected that a Competent Person will review site-standard fall
protection and rescue procedures each and every time work begins. However, the
Competent Person should review these procedures frequently enough to ensure
that the implementation of the program is correct and that authorized persons are
adequately informed about the fall protection and rescue procedures of the task
they are performing.
For nonstandard work at elevation, the Competent Person must be directly
involved in all aspects of planning, implementing, and monitoring the nonstandard
job.
Competent persons are encouraged to become Certified Safety Professionals
(www.bcsp.org) to add breadth to their qualifications.
The Qualified Person
Also presently required is the appointment of a Qualified Person, ideally a
representative of the structural or mechanical branch of engineering, to assist
in eliminating or controlling fall hazards at the design and planning stages of
each new construction and maintenance project. This Qualified Person must be
thoroughly familiar with state-of-the-art fall protection equipment and design
practices. Outside consultants may be employed to fill this roll at sites that do not
have qualified fall protection engineers.

is a term that involves judgment in making a decision. Decisions made based upon
risk generally come far short of protecting 100 percent of the working population.
Not everyone will be protected when some theoretical level of risk is deemed to be

Instead of the word risk the word hazard should be used when communicating

The author believes it is the duty of an organization, particularly its safety

Fall hazards involving outside contractors or visitors to a business (inspectors,

Once a fall hazard is identified by an organization, it should not leave the open

Identifying Hazardous Exposures
Fall-hazard analysis begins by listing the work tasks that involve or could involve
exposure to an elevated fall hazard. It is important to reemphasize that this should
include travel. For example, a valve that must be monitored regularly is located in
an elevated pipe rack and requires vertical and horizontal mobility for access and
egress, but the actual work task may be stationary. Other elevated work, such as
painting or sandblasting, may require more mobility.
